title: Book Eleven opens: the priesthood of the law as a type of Christ's
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK ELEVEN. On the priesthood, and that the priesthood under the law was a type of the priesthood in Christ.

Cyril: We have now completed a sufficient discussion of the tabernacle and of the oracles given concerning it, polished very well and elegantly to a spiritual subtlety. Now it would be fitting, as it seems to me (and you yourself will agree, I know), to take up the honors of the priesthood, and the way in which the true priesthood is signified through the priesthood in type and under the law: that is, the priesthood which, in Christ and through him, sanctifies the sacred race. By the sacred race I mean, once again, those who have been made radiant in faith and enriched with closeness to God through sharing in the Holy Spirit.
Palladius: It would indeed be fitting, and very rightly so.

Cyril: When the holy tabernacle had been finished with fitting adornment, and brought into the form shown on the mountain to the inspired Moses (Exodus 25:40), God went on to appoint the priests. He said (Exodus 28:1): ‘And you, bring near to yourself Aaron your brother and his sons
translator_notes: Source block breaks mid-quotation after ἐκ; the quotation of Exodus 28:1 is completed at the start of section 2, so the citation is placed before the quotation here and again at its close in section 2. 'The form shown on the mountain' alludes to Exodus 25:40 LXX (κατὰ τὸν τύπον τὸν δεδειγμένον σοι ἐν τῷ ὄρει); cited as a clear allusion. 'The sacred race' (τὸ ἱερὸν γένος) may echo 1 Peter 2:9 (γένος ἐκλεκτόν, ἱεράτευμα), but the wording differs; left uncited. θεσπέσιος rendered 'inspired' throughout (of Moses, the disciples, Paul). 'In spirit and truth' in the title is the work's title formula from John 4:23-24; not cited in the reading text. Cyril's 'when the tabernacle had been finished' is his own ordering of the material: in Exodus the command to appoint the priests (ch. 28) comes before the account of the building (chs. 35-40).

title: Called by name: Aaron as a type of Christ the High Priest
english: Cyril: …from among the sons of Israel, to serve me as priests: Aaron, and Nadab and Abihu, and Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron.’ (Exodus 28:1) So the chosen men were called by name to the sacred ministry. For ‘no one takes the honor for himself, but the one who is called by God’ (Hebrews 5:4), as it is written. Let no one, then, go of his own accord into serving God as a priest; let him wait for a call. Otherwise, if he tries to seize what he does not hold by decree from above, he will suffer the punishment of Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16:31–33). And do not be surprised that self-appointment is out of place and unseemly among us, when Paul writes even about Christ himself: ‘He did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him, “You are a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchizedek”’ (Hebrews 5:5–6; Psalm 110:4). So what was wisely said to Moses would again be an image of the call spoken of in Christ’s case: ‘And you, bring near to yourself Aaron your brother and his sons’ (Exodus 28:1). For what else does ‘bring near’ mean than ‘make him your own and call him to you’? Now Christ has been called, as it were, to be high priest through the counsel of the Father. And in a certain way the inspired disciples were also called together with him and made fellow workers for the sacred ministry. That is why they said plainly, ‘For we are God’s fellow workers’ (1 Corinthians 3:9); and they went about the whole world under the sun, serving the Gospel of Christ as priests among the nations (Romans 15:16). They were indeed called to apostleship through Christ, and the statement is true. But this too was surely willed by the Father; for there is one decision over all that is done, since the Son is the counsel and wisdom and will of the Father. So Aaron would be a type of Christ, and, as it were, a showing in advance of the priesthood understood in spirit and truth, as still in the dimmer shadows. Notice that Moses is commanded to bring Aaron near to himself; for the law is in some way weak and incomplete if it is separated from Christ. ‘For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins’ (Hebrews 10:4). But Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sinners, has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:12, 14). Let those, then, who are still friends of the shadow and the letter, and who have been counted worthy of the commandments of Moses, know this: unless they bring near to themselves the high priest and apostle of our confession, Jesus Christ (Hebrews 3:1), their zeal for the worship in type will come to nothing. For what would the boasts of life under the law amount to before God, who loves virtue? That is why our most wise Paul says that, because of the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of Christ, he counts the things in the world as refuse (Philippians 3:8), and has chosen spiritual things instead. And this, understood spiritually, is to bring Aaron himself near to oneself.
Palladius: I understand what you say; the point is clear.
Cyril: ‘Bring near to yourself,’ then, he says,
translator_notes: Continuation of the Exodus 28:1 quotation begun in section 1. Hebrews 5:5-6: Cyril omits the intervening 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you' and runs 5:5 into 5:6; the quoted oracle is Psalm 109:4 LXX = Psalm 110:4 in English Bibles. 'it was he who said to him' renders the elliptical ἀλλ' ὁ λαλήσας πρὸς αὐτόν without supplying a verb. Dathan and Abiram: the punishment (the earth opening) is Numbers 16:31-33; cited as a clear allusion (cf. also Psalm 106:17). 'Serving the Gospel of Christ as priests among the nations' echoes Romans 15:16 (ἱερουργοῦντα τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ... εἰς τὰ ἔθνη), where Paul speaks of the Gospel 'of God'; cited as a clear allusion. Hebrews 10:12 reads 'for sins' (ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν); Cyril's text has ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτωλῶν 'for sinners', kept. Hebrews 3:1 has 'apostle and high priest'; Cyril reverses the order, kept. 'Counsel and wisdom and will of the Father' may echo 1 Corinthians 1:24 (Christ the wisdom of God); uncited. 'In spirit and truth' (John 4:23-24) is the work's title formula; uncited. κατηξιωμένοι rendered literally 'who were counted worthy of' the commandments of Moses.

title: Aaron given to weak Moses as a type of Christ; the holy robe is Christ
english: Cyril: …‘Aaron your brother’ (Exodus 28:1), in another sense too, I think, since he knew that the matter is not without value for the benefit that comes through spiritual understanding. Consider what I mean. Moses was being sent to bring Israel out of their misery in Egypt. Then, seeing that the undertaking rose far above human power and beyond the measure of the strength and eloquence he had, he pleaded, saying: ‘Look, I have not been eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant; I am weak in voice and slow of tongue’ (Exodus 4:10). When God answered him, ‘Who gave man a mouth? Who made the deaf and the mute, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God? Now go, and I will open your mouth’ (Exodus 4:11–12), Moses, overcome by the greatness of the deeds to be achieved, was afraid again and said: ‘I beg you, Lord, appoint another who is able, whom you will send’ (Exodus 4:13). Then God at once appointed Aaron (Exodus 4:14–16), as a type of Christ, who knows how to accomplish all things with ease. And Israel was redeemed in no other way than by Christ being given, once again as in the image of Aaron, as a fellow worker to the halting speech and weakness of Moses. You will understand the present passage in the same way. For God, perfecting the weakness of the law in Christ, brought Aaron into the priesthood and joins him to good purpose with the blessed Moses. For the law would not suffice for redemption, nor would it be able to perfect the redeemed in sanctification. But Christ is redemption and sanctification (1 Corinthians 1:30), with the saints working together with him; just as Moses then worked with Aaron in Egypt, and the sons worked with Aaron himself. So too the inspired disciples worked together, in the spiritual sense, with Christ, the high priest and leader of all. He has power to accomplish all things, and they did not assist him as one who was weak; they were called to serve and chosen as the best, and from him they gained strength for everything. The inspired Paul will bear witness to this when he says: ‘I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me’ (Philippians 4:13).
Palladius: So Aaron and the rest were chosen and called by name to the sacred ministry.

Cyril: And besides this he ordained that splendid garments, fit for sacred service, should be made for them, saying: ‘And you shall make a holy robe for Aaron your brother, for honor and glory. And you, speak to all who are wise in understanding, whom I have filled with a spirit of perception, and they shall make the holy robe for Aaron for the sanctuary, in which he will serve me as priest’ (Exodus 28:2–3). Now the most wise Paul advises those who have been justified in faith that they must put on the robe that is truly holy and from heaven, writing: ‘Put on our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 13:14). This is what the prophet Isaiah cried out beforehand, speaking as in the person of the Church: ‘Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness’ (Isaiah 61:10). The garment, then, that is for
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation (end of the repeated Exodus 28:1 phrase). εἰδὼς has God as subject ('he says ... knowing'); rendered 'since he knew'. Exodus 4:10 LXX reads οὐχ ἱκανός ('not able/fit'); Cyril's text has οὐκ εὔλαλος ('not eloquent'), kept. Exodus 4:13 quoted closely from the LXX. 'God at once appointed Aaron' summarises Exodus 4:14-16 (Aaron as Moses' spokesman); cited as a clear allusion. 'Christ is redemption and sanctification' echoes 1 Corinthians 1:30 (ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις); cited as a clear allusion. Philippians 4:13: Cyril's text includes 'Christ', as in many manuscripts. Romans 13:14: Cyril's text adds 'our' (ἡμῶν), kept. Isaiah 61:10 follows the LXX (χιτῶνα εὐφροσύνης 'tunic of gladness'). Exodus 28:2-3 follows the LXX ('spirit of perception', 'for the sanctuary'). ἀνάπτεσθαι ('fasten on oneself') rendered 'put on' to match the Pauline verb that follows. Section ends mid-sentence; completed in section 4.

title: Christ the garment of glory; the colors of the robe show the Word
english: Cyril: …honor and glory, in truth, for the sacred and holy race is Christ, a splendid adornment, beyond this world, for the souls of the saints. ‘For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ’ (Galatians 3:27), he says, and the saying is true. But the law adorns Aaron as in shadows, referring to Christ the glory that comes from his richly varied robes. For a mystical and exact meaning is found all but woven into the making of these works of craft, hinting in riddles at the glory of the Savior. See how he says that the makers of the garments were filled with understanding from God (Exodus 28:3), since God was leading them to richly colored embroidery and writing the glory of Christ into the vestments. The pieces to be made were the breastpiece and the ephod, the full-length robe and the fringed tunic, the turban and the sash (Exodus 28:4): these, and others besides, which we will discuss one by one as far as we can. He spoke, then, of the materials taken for the work: ‘And they shall take the gold, and the blue, and the purple, and the scarlet, and fine linen’ (Exodus 28:5). Now once more, please, bring a keen mind to what lies before us, and first of all observe this.
Palladius: What do you mean?
Cyril: Were not all the things in the tabernacle made of gold and fine linen, and also of purple and spun scarlet, and of blue? And were they not a type of Christ?
Palladius: That is so.

Cyril: See, then, that the robe of the one who holds first place in the priesthood was made of the same materials, again laboring, as in an image and in types, to bring forth the glory of Christ. For the same meanings, and no different knowledge, point to the beauty of Christ. He is known as God in the gold; as having royal dignity in the purple; as the fine and bodiless Word in the fine linen; in the scarlet, because of the flesh; and in the blue, which looks like the sky (for that is the color of hyacinth), because he is from above and from heaven. Or is not the Word who is from God the Father both God and King at once?
Palladius: How could he not be?
Cyril: And though he is the fine and bodiless Word of the Father, did he not come to be in flesh? And is he not from above?
Palladius: True.

Cyril: So, to careful contemplation, the materials of the garments are exactly the same as those of the things made in the holy tabernacle. So much for that. Now it is time to speak of the things woven in many colors for Aaron’s honor and glory. So he says (Exodus 28:6–8): ‘And they shall make the ephod of spun fine linen, the woven work of an embroiderer. It shall have two shoulder pieces joined to each other, fastened at its two edges. And the woven work of the
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence (completing 'The garment, then, that is for' from section 3) and ends mid-quotation of Exodus 28:8 (τὸ ὕφασμα τῶν [ἐπωμίδων]); the citation for the split quotation is placed before it. The garment list follows Exodus 28:4 LXX exactly (περιστήθιον, ἐπωμίς, ποδήρης, χιτὼν κοσυμβωτός, κίδαρις, ζώνη). ἐπωμίς is rendered 'ephod' for the garment and 'shoulder pieces' for the two straps of Exodus 28:7, since the LXX uses the one word for both. ὑάκινθος rendered 'blue' (the usual English for the color), with 'hyacinth' kept where Cyril explains the color. 'Filled with understanding from God' refers back to Exodus 28:3 quoted in section 3; cited. The question 'Were not all the things in the tabernacle made of gold and fine linen...' summarises the tabernacle materials (cf. Exodus 25:3-4; 26:1) rather than quoting one verse; left uncited. 'From above and from heaven' may echo John 3:31; 'came to be in flesh' may echo John 1:14; both wording differs, left uncited. λόγος ἰσχνὸς καὶ ἀσώματος is capitalised 'Word', since the next exchange names the Λόγος τοῦ Πατρὸς λεπτὸς καὶ ἀσώματος.

title: The ephod’s emerald stones, an image of heaven
english: Cyril: …of the shoulder pieces, which is on it, shall be of one piece with it in its workmanship, of gold and blue and purple and spun scarlet and twisted fine linen’ (Exodus 28:8). Having given the woven work the material already named, he goes straight on: ‘And you shall take the two stones, emerald stones, and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel, six names on the one stone and the remaining six names on the second stone, according to their birth. As the work of the stonecutter’s craft, as the engraving of a seal, you shall engrave the stones with the names of the sons of Israel. And you shall set the two stones on the shoulders of the ephod; they are stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel’ (Exodus 28:9–12).
Palladius: The meaning in these contemplations runs deep, it seems. But first try to tell me this: what is the thing called the ephod, and how would it have been made?

Cyril: He commanded that a woven garment be made, shaped like a tunic and reaching down to the chest, laid over the garments beneath it, those worn next to the skin that reach to the feet, so that, flashing with the gleam of gold and purple, it might stir in the eyes of those who saw it a wonder both august and fitting for holy things. He called it the ephod, that is, the shoulder piece, because, I think, the work was short and barely stretched across both shoulders. On this ephod, then, he plainly prescribed that two stones be set, stones of emerald, bound very tightly with fine threads, with the names of the tribes skilfully engraved on them, so that six were written on one stone. And the reason for this he himself made plain to us when he said: ‘And Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel before the Lord on his two shoulders, a remembrance for them’ (Exodus 28:12).
Palladius: And what, once again, shall we take the stones and what is on them to signify?

Cyril: Listen, then. The emerald is a pale stone. Deep within it something bright swims, and light is blended, as it were, with darkness, each drawing the victory toward itself against the other. Well then, Palladius, when the bodily eye looks up to the heights above and strains into the depths toward the upper air and heaven, will it not meet with just such a sight? For the uppermost air, very high above, is pale, I think, dark as it were in its depths, and mingled with a moderate light.
Palladius: That is so.

Cyril: So holy Scripture makes the stone an image of heaven. And do not be surprised when it likens heaven, in turn, to sapphire; for sapphire too is pale, and not far from the look of emerald. It is written thus in Exodus: ‘And Moses went up, and Aaron, and Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel. And they saw the place where the God of Israel stood; and what was under his feet was like a work of sapphire stone, and like the appearance of the firmament of heaven in its purity’ (Exodus 24:9–10).
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation of Exodus 28:8 (LXX; English numbering the same); begun in section 4. LXX 'emerald' (σμάραγδος) for Hebrew shoham (usually 'onyx'); kept as emerald because Cyril's whole reading turns on the stone's color. ὑάκινθος rendered 'blue' (the violet-blue dye; older English 'hyacinth'). ἐπωμίς is explained by Cyril from ὦμος, 'shoulder', so it is given once as 'the ephod, that is, the shoulder piece'. λήψεται ('shall take') in Exodus 28:12 rendered 'shall bear', its sense in context. In the Exodus 24:10 quotation Cyril reads λίθου ('stone') where the LXX has πλίνθου ('brick'); English follows Cyril. In 'likens heaven to sapphire' the pronoun αὐτόν is masculine and refers to οὐρανός (heaven); made explicit. ὠχρός rendered 'pale' (a pale, yellowish-green pallor); αἰθήρ rendered 'upper air'.

title: Names written in heaven, carried on Christ’s shoulders
english: Cyril: For since the Israelites, while they lived in Egypt, had served the creation (Romans 1:25) and called heaven a god, the Lord of all appeared to them, for their good, standing upon the firmament itself, so that they might know that he has all things under his feet and is master of the heavens themselves, as their Creator. Do you see, then, that holy Scripture makes the stone, with its pallor as of a moderate light, a kind of type and image of heaven? For by nature it gleams dark blue.
Palladius: Very well said.

Cyril: The emerald, then, is a sign of heaven. It has Israel written on it, family by family, and it has been given the ephod as its place. From this we may understand that those who have been granted enrollment in heaven will surely, and in every way, rest upon Christ, who all but carries them on his shoulders and counts the good in the rank of children. The divine Moses said something like this when he adorned Israel with the tender care that comes from God: ‘As an eagle would shelter its nest, and yearned over its young, spreading its wings it received them, and took them up on its back’ (Deuteronomy 32:11). David too sings to every holy one who has made his dwelling in the help of the Most High (Psalm 91:1): ‘He will overshadow you upon his back,’ he says (Psalm 91:4). By ‘back’ I take him to mean the parts just below the neck, the region, as it were, of the shoulders, and not the back as a whole. So, in the words of the prophet, they will be lifted up on shoulders (Isaiah 60:4; Isaiah 66:12), and, as with Ephraim of old, they will be taken up on the arm (Hosea 11:3): those who have been granted the enrollment above. The Savior himself declared that enrollment glorious and admirable, surpassing even the beauty of the divine gifts, when he said somewhere to the holy disciples: ‘Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you, but rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven’ (Luke 10:20). And he says that the enrollment on the stones will be a remembrance for the sons of Israel before the Lord (Exodus 28:12), who all but fixes his gaze on them, as they are in Aaron. For God the Father receives us into remembrance in Christ, and in him we have become known to God and worthy of his watchful care, as though written in God’s book.
Palladius: Rightly said.

Cyril: He commands that yet another ornament be added to it, saying: ‘And you shall make little shields of pure gold, of mingled work, and you shall make two fringes of pure gold, mingled with flowers, a plaited work; and you shall put the plaited fringes on the little shields and on their shoulder straps at the front. And you shall make the oracle of judgments, the work of a weaver, after the design of the ephod; you shall make it of gold and blue and purple and twisted scarlet and twisted fine linen. You shall make it square; it shall be double, a span its length and a span its breadth’ (Exodus 28:13–16), ‘and you shall weave into it a woven work set with…
translator_notes: 'Served the creation' (λελατρεύκασι τῇ κτίσει) echoes the wording of Romans 1:25 (ἐλάτρευσαν τῇ κτίσει) and is cited as a clear verbal allusion. 'All things under his feet' may echo Psalm 8:6 but is left uncited (doubtful). 'For by nature it gleams dark blue' (κυαναυγὴς γὰρ φύσει): the subject is unstated in Greek; it may be the stone or heaven; English keeps it open. Psalm 91:1 and 91:4 are LXX Psalm 90:1 and 90:4 (converted to English numbering). LXX μετάφρενα means the upper back between the shoulders; rendered 'back' so that Cyril's following explanation makes sense. 'Lifted up on shoulders' (ἐπ' ὤμων ἀρθήσονται) matches the LXX wording of both Isaiah 60:4 and Isaiah 66:12; Cyril names only 'the prophet', so both are given. 'Taken up on the arm, as with Ephraim' = Hosea 11:3 LXX (ἀνέλαβον αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τὸν βραχίονά μου). In Luke 10:20 Cyril writes 'the demons' where Luke has 'the spirits' (cf. Luke 10:17); English follows Cyril. 'Enrollment in heaven' may also recall Hebrews 12:23 and 'God's book' the book of life (Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5); both uncited as doubtful. ὡδίπη read as ὧδέ πῃ ('thus somewhere'). In the Exodus 28:13 quotation Cyril's text applies καταμεμιγμένας ('mixed') to the little shields as well as the fringes; rendered 'of mingled work'. ἀσπιδίσκαι kept as 'little shields' because Cyril later reads them as the armor of God; κροσσωτά kept as 'fringes' because Cyril later explains them as chains and links them to Psalm 45:13. λόγιον τῶν κρίσεων ('breastpiece' in Hebrew-based Bibles) kept as 'oracle of judgments' because Cyril builds an etymology on λόγιον in sections 7–8. 'A remembrance ... before the Lord' paraphrases Exodus 28:12 and is cited there. In the Exodus 28:15 quotation κοκκίνου κεκλωσμένου is 'twisted scarlet' (section 5's διανενησμένου was 'spun scarlet'). The quotation (Exodus 28:17) runs over into section 7.

title: How the oracle of judgments was made
english: Cyril: …stones, in four rows’ (Exodus 28:17). Then, after setting out the names of the stones, he adds again: ‘And let the stones be twelve, according to the names of the sons of Israel, according to their names; let them be engravings of seals, each according to their names, for the twelve tribes’ (Exodus 28:21). And next, a little further on, he says: ‘And Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel on the oracle of judgment, on his breast, when he goes into the Holy Place, a remembrance before the Lord God’ (Exodus 28:29).
Palladius: How deep a matter the oracle is! Even the way it was made seems to me very hard to grasp.

Cyril: We must approach it, then, and come as near the truth as we can, even if the steep climb perhaps does not allow us to reach it entirely. For to see very obscure things even in a mirror (1 Corinthians 13:12) is, I would say, better than the alternative, I mean, than not to have grasped them at all. I will speak, then, as far as possible, and as I am able to understand it. He commanded that two little shields be made of pure gold, wider than the round of a coin but of the same shape, for a coin is round; then two fringes of pure gold, mingled with flowers. By the fringes we mean chains, whose appearance is richly varied, as with colors, for by ‘flowers’ he meant colors. These colors, then, were fine linen and purple, and gold thread, and blue as well, and the scarlet yarn. Besides this, he says that a square woven piece must be made, shaped, as it were, like a cube, a span in size and equal on every side. And he says that the twelve stones must be woven very firmly into it, set three by three, in four rows in all, with the names of the tribes engraved on them. So the little shields hung from the ephod by golden chains of many kinds, though they sat a little lower than the height of the shoulders themselves. They touched the chest and hung right over the breasts. And from the little shields, by other chains, the oracle of judgments, firmly attached, rested lightly on the chest, with the fringes hanging down. To those who saw it the thing was no small marvel, bright with stones and gold, and gloriously worked in the fine colors of the other materials. This too, he says, will again be a remembrance for the sons of Israel before the Lord, when Aaron goes into the Holy Place (Exodus 28:29). Is the shape of these works now as clear to you as it can be?
Palladius: Very clear. But why is the name ‘the oracle of judgments’ given to this work?
Cyril: Did we not say, explaining the word’s origin, that the upper piece was called the ephod, the shoulder piece, because it is stretched over both shoulders?
Palladius: Yes. What of it?
Cyril: That, again, by true derivation and by analogy, we say that the piece laid up, as it were…
translator_notes: The source reads κατὰ τὸν λίθον τετράστιχον, apparently a corruption of the LXX κατάλιθον τετράστιχον ('set with stones, in four rows', Exodus 28:17); English follows the LXX sense. Exodus 28:29 LXX lacks the Hebrew 28:23–28 but keeps the verse number 29; Cyril's text has 'Lord God' where the LXX has 'God'. λήψεται again rendered 'shall bear'. 'See even in a mirror' (ἐν ἐσόπτρῳ βλέπειν) is cited as a clear allusion to 1 Corinthians 13:12. ὑπεκάθηντο μέντοι ἠρέμα, τὸ ὑψοῦ τε δοκεῖν καὶ ἐπ' αὐτοῖς εἶναι τοῖς ὤμοις is hard: taken as 'sat a little lower than seeming to be high up on the shoulders themselves', i.e. the little shields hung somewhat below the shoulder line; doubtful. κροσσωτῶν ἐκκεκρεμασμένων (genitive absolute) kept as 'with the fringes hanging down'; the fringes are the 'other chains' by which the oracle hangs from the little shields. The litotes οὐκ ἀθαύμαστον kept as 'no small marvel'. ἐπωμίς again explained as 'the ephod, the shoulder piece' because Cyril points back to his derivation from ὦμος. 'This too will be a remembrance' paraphrases Exodus 28:29 and is cited again. The sentence on the name runs over into section 8.

title: The oracle on the heart: right judgment and the armor of God
english: Cyril: …in the heart and the inward parts has been named the oracle (logion) of judgments. For the heart and the inward parts are, so to speak, the dwelling place of the reason (logikon) within us. And firmly set, and as it were naturally fixed, in the reason within us is also right and blameless judgment about each thing to be done, that is, just judgment, and what befits each case. Or is it not some power of reason in us that weighs the nature of the things to be done, and separates what is unpleasant and unprofitable from what is better?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: It is the custom of the divinely inspired Scripture to call uprightness and just judgment ‘judgment’. So the divine David sings: ‘Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times’ (Psalm 106:3). And again he said somewhere: ‘And the honor of the king loves judgment’ (Psalm 99:4). For the honor and glory of a king is splendid when it loves righteousness. So, then, the piece laid upon the heart and breast is the oracle of judgment, because it lies, as it were, in the place of the reason, where uprightness in righteousness is found. On it are twelve stones set round with gold, bearing an inscription: the tribes. They would be a type of holy men, who are splendid and precious, like choice stones, lying, as it were, in the mind and heart of Christ. And they are truly worthy of remembrance, because of the brightness of their virtue and the worth of their sanctification. Golden fringes also hang from the oracle of judgments. The thing indicates, I think, that the great and countless host of noble deeds done by the multitude of the saints is seen, as it were, hanging from it. And indeed the blessed David says that the adornment of the Church is in fringes (Psalm 45:13).
Palladius: The account is convincing.

Cyril: From the oracle of judgments, gripped by golden clasps, a many-colored and bright chain climbs upward, as we were saying, and passing through both little shields, it reaches the very top of the ephod, where the stones of the enrollment are. Is it not worth seeing what this, too, might mean? To me the riddle seems again to point to something like this: that the precious stones, which are in the knowledge and the memory of Christ, as they run toward the enrollment above, gain it through the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left (2 Corinthians 6:7); for so the divine Paul plainly writes. And elsewhere he also says: ‘Put on the whole armor of God’ (Ephesians 6:11). A king’s weapons are golden, and golden likewise are the little shields, which hint, as in a riddle, at the whole armor of God. So we shall be in God’s memory and enrollment in no other way than by taking up the weapons of righteousness and making our way by them in action. And its being fastened to the ephod…
translator_notes: Cyril derives λόγιον ('oracle', the LXX name for the breastpiece) from τὸ λογικόν, the reasoning faculty; the Greek words are shown once in parentheses so the wordplay can be seen. LXX Psalm numbering converted: Psalm 105:3 LXX = Psalm 106:3; Psalm 98:4 LXX = Psalm 99:4; Psalm 44:14 LXX ('clothed in golden fringes', ἐν κροσσωτοῖς χρυσοῖς) = Psalm 45:13. The source prints the Psalm 99:4 verb as ἀγαπᾷν (infinitive) and never closes the quotation marks; the quotation is taken to end at 'loves judgment' (LXX ἀγαπᾷ), and 'For splendid is the honor…' is Cyril's own gloss. κρωσσοί in section 8 is a variant spelling of κροσσοί ('tassels, fringes'); rendered 'fringes' to match κροσσωτά. δάκτυλοι ('fingers') rendered 'clasps' (gripping pieces) rather than 'rings', since the word is not δακτύλιοι; doubtful wording. 'Running toward the enrollment above' may recall Philippians 3:14; uncited as doubtful. 'Choice stones' may recall 1 Peter 2:4–6 (λίθος ἐκλεκτός, a different word); uncited. 'A king's weapons' is lowercase: Cyril states a general point, though the king may be Christ. The negation in 'in no other way than' keeps οὐχ ἑτέρως … μὴ οὐχί. The section breaks off mid-sentence; it continues in section 9.

title: The oracle joins earth to heaven; Manifestation and Truth
english: Cyril: …the oracle would signify, I think, that the things below are joined to the things above, with Christ as mediator. ‘For he himself is our peace, who has made both one’ (Ephesians 2:14), as the Scriptures say; and he has bound humankind to the multitude of the holy angels by the bond of love. It should be known, too, that the blessed Ezekiel says that the ruler of Tyre was clothed with every precious stone (Ezekiel 28:13); and he lists the very stones which the inspired Moses says were set in the oracle of judgment. They were these: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire and jasper, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl and onyx (Exodus 28:17–20). They were arranged in threes, in four rows in all, and this arrangement sketches for us the firmness in faith of those who are in the heart and memory of Christ. For the setting in threes is a symbol of faith, as in the Trinity; and the arrangement as in a square figure with equal sides is a symbol of firmness. For the oracle on which the twelve stones were set was made in this way (Exodus 28:16).
Palladius: I am persuaded.

Cyril: Besides these, he also orders something else to be joined with the twelve stones, saying: ‘And you shall put on the oracle of judgment the Manifestation and the Truth, and it shall be on Aaron’s breast whenever he goes into the holy place before the Lord; and Aaron shall bring the judgments of the sons of Israel on the breast before the Lord continually’ (Exodus 28:30). He names them Manifestation and Truth, but he does not go on to state clearly whether he ordered them to be stones, or writing as on a small tablet. But I will call to mind the prophet who says, ‘For the sons of Israel shall sit many days with no king and no ruler, with no sacrifice and no altar, with neither priesthood nor manifestations’ (Hosea 3:4). But whether these too were stones, or the names were written in gold as on a tablet, our discussion will not inquire into it too closely. We shall recognize, however, that they were set there as a type of Christ’s presence with the saints. ‘For behold,’ he says, ‘I am with you always, to the end of the age’ (Matthew 28:20). And Christ is the Truth and the Manifestation. For in him we have come to know the Father, and he has made known to us his good will, perfect and pleasing, as the Scriptures say (Romans 12:2). For Christ said somewhere, ‘I no longer call you servants; you are my friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have declared to you’ (John 15:14–15). Emmanuel is the Truth in another sense as well: because he alone is Son by nature, and, as God from God, he alone is holy, he alone is Lord; while creation is, by participation and by imitation, whatever he himself is understood to be. So Christ, understood as Manifestation and Truth, is with the saints; and he brings our affairs before the face of the Father (Hebrews 9:24), since he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). For this, I think, is the meaning of ‘And Aaron shall bring the judgments of the sons of Israel…’ (Exodus 28:30)
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence: PG 68.740 ends 'Τὸ δὲ δὴ τῆς ἐπωμίδος ἀνῆφθαι' and §9 continues 'τὸ λόγιον κατασημήνειεν ἂν'. Whole sentence: 'And the fastening of the oracle to the ephod would signify, I think, that the things below are joined to the things above.' Whoever joins §8 to §9 should check that the end of §8 reads into '…the oracle would signify'. λόγιον (LXX 'oracle', the high priest's breastpiece) kept as 'oracle' because Cyril's reading of 'oracle of judgment' in §8 depends on the word; λόγιον τῶν κρίσεων 'oracle of judgment'. Stone names follow the LXX of Exodus 28:17–20 in the usual English forms (sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, onyx). The arrangement 'in four rows' is Exodus 28:17 (covered by the 28:17–20 citation). Ezekiel 28:13 LXX lists the same twelve stones (plus silver and gold) for the ruler (LXX ἄρχων) of Tyre; Cyril's 'he lists these' refers to Ezekiel. Exodus 28:16 cited for the square shape ('square ... a span long and a span wide'). δήλωσις καὶ ἀλήθεια = the Urim and Thummim of the Hebrew text; rendered 'Manifestation and Truth' because Cyril reads the LXX names. Hosea 3:4 LXX has δήλων ('manifestations', Hebrew teraphim); Cyril cites it as another place where the same object is named, so 'manifestations' keeps the link to 'Manifestation'. Exodus 28:30: Cyril's text has εἰσοίσει ('shall bring in'); the closing quotation runs across into §10, so the citation stands at the break in both sections. 'We have come to know the Father in him' may echo John 14:7–9; left uncited as a loose allusion. 'Bond of love' may echo Colossians 3:14 (σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος); not cited, wording differs. 'Alone holy, alone Lord' resembles Revelation 15:4 and the Gloria; not cited. Hebrews 9:24 cited for 'before the face of the Father' (ἐμφανισθῆναι τῷ προσώπῳ τοῦ θεοῦ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν); Hebrews 7:25 quoted nearly verbatim ('ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν' for 'ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν'). John 15:14–15: Cyril blends 'you are my friends' (15:14) with 15:15 and has ἀπήγγειλα for ἐγνώρισα. 'μεθεκτῶς ... καὶ κατὰ μίμησιν': creation has holiness and lordship only by participation and imitation, Christ by nature; kept exact.

title: The blue robe: incorruption from above
english: Cyril: …before the Lord on his breast continually’ (Exodus 28:30).
Palladius: True.

Cyril: He orders that a vestment be made, fit for a priest and worthy of admiration, saying: ‘And you shall make a full-length robe, all of blue. Its opening for the head shall be in the middle of it, with a border all around the opening, woven work, the joining woven together from the same piece, so that it may not be torn. And beneath the hem of the robe, below, you shall make little pomegranates like those of a pomegranate in bloom, of blue and purple and spun scarlet and twisted fine linen, beneath the hem of the robe all around. Of the same pattern as the pomegranates, golden bells between them all around: beside each pomegranate a golden bell and a flower, on the hem of the robe all around. And when Aaron ministers, its sound shall be heard as he goes into the holy place before the Lord and as he comes out, so that he may not die’ (Exodus 28:31–35). By ‘full-length robe’ he clearly means a long tunic, well suited to cover the body, reaching from the neck itself to the tips of the feet. It is of blue because this is a symbol of the incorruption from above, that is, of Christ. For the inspired David too proclaimed something of this kind beforehand, speaking as in the person of God about those who serve as priests in the churches: ‘Her priests I will clothe with salvation’ (Psalm 132:16). And the wise Paul writes to us, ‘Put on our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 13:14). And this, I think, is our dwelling from heaven, which we long to put on (2 Corinthians 5:2), the tunic of gladness, the garment of salvation, as the prophet says (Isaiah 61:10). It has been clearly stated that the color blue is a figure of heaven. This account is true when it is applied to ourselves, for we have been clothed with the incorruption from above. But if Christ himself should be understood as the one wearing the full-length robe, as in the person of Aaron, our account is no less true. For the Only-begotten, being God by nature, makes his own body incorruptible; and, clothing it with the life from above, he set it entirely beyond the greed of death. That incorruption and life are in Christ by nature, and not by participation, you will understand from this as well. For, as one who is God by nature, he said, ‘I am the resurrection and the life’ (John 11:25). But as one who is given life in respect of his humanity, he says, ‘For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself’ (John 5:26). So even if Christ himself is understood as the one said to be clothed with the incorruption from above, the interpretation would not stray from what is fitting. On the lower parts are pomegranates and bells, set alternately: the pomegranates woven in, and the bells of gold, so that they would truly ring out well, and, when Aaron hurries into the Holy of Holies, would make his entrance very noticeable. This too is a symbol of the saving and wise dispensation; I mean of the divine Gospel…
translator_notes: Opens with the end of the Exodus 28:30 quotation that began at the close of §9; Cyril's second form adds αὐτοῦ ('his breast'). ὑποδύτης ποδήρης 'full-length robe' (LXX 'undergarment reaching to the feet'); ὑάκινθος/ὑακίνθινος rendered 'blue' throughout (the violet-blue dye; older English 'hyacinth'), since Cyril reads it as the color of heaven. ᾤα 'border', συμβολή 'joining', λῶμα 'hem', ἄνθινον 'flower'. Cyril's text of Exodus 28:33 reads 'Τὸ αὐτὸ εἶδος τοῖς ῥοΐσκοις, καὶ κώδωνας χρυσοῦς' ('of the same pattern as the pomegranates, golden bells'), which differs slightly from the Rahlfs LXX ('ῥοΐσκους χρυσοῦς καὶ κώδωνας'); translated as Cyril has it. Psalm 131:16 LXX = Psalm 132:16 in English Bibles ('αὐτῆς' = Zion's priests). Isaiah 61:10 LXX has both 'garment of salvation' and 'tunic of gladness'. 2 Corinthians 5:2: Cyril has ἐνδύσασθαι for Paul's ἐπενδύσασθαι. 'We have been clothed with the incorruption from above' may echo 1 Corinthians 15:53–54; not cited (tense and setting differ). 'It has been clearly stated that blue is a figure of heaven' refers back to earlier books of this work, not to Scripture; uncited. Doctrinal terms kept exact: φυσικῶς ... καὶ ἀμεθέκτως 'by nature, and not by participation'; ζωοποιούμενος κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον 'given life in respect of his humanity' (Cyril's distinction between what the Word has as God and receives as man). τυχόν rendered 'as it happens' (it softens the description of the hem). Cyril says the bells mark Aaron's entry into 'the Holy of Holies', though Exodus 28:35 has 'the holy place'; kept as Cyril wrote. Section ends mid-sentence ('φημὶ δὴ τοῦ θείου τε καὶ εὐαγγελικοῦ' | §11 'κηρύγματος'): 'I mean of the divine Gospel…' + §11 '…proclamation'.

title: Bells and pomegranates: teachers in every city; the gold plate
english: Cyril: …proclamation, which rings out, as it were, around every city, when our great high priest (Hebrews 4:14), the spotless victim, has entered for our sake into the Holy of Holies, having obtained eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12). ‘For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified’ (Hebrews 10:14). The riddle is not hard to see through: the bells made of gold stand for the saving proclamation, and the pomegranates for cities.
Palladius: In what way?

Cyril: A city is enclosed on the outside by a single wall, yet holds countless quarters within itself. In the same way, I think, the pomegranate fruit is girded on the outside by a single rind, while inside the seeds are walled off from one another by thin membranes and are all but gathered into quarters. Or is it not so?
Palladius: I agree.

Cyril: So there is a bell beside each pomegranate, for there is a teacher in each city, who by the ringing and clear sound of the divine doctrines makes our Savior’s entry into the Holy of Holies plain to all. And the fear of death hangs over those appointed to serve as priests, that is, over Aaron, as he goes into the holy tabernacle, unless the strokes of the bells ring out loudly all around. For silence is a dangerous thing for teachers. And this is plainly what Paul said: ‘For woe to me if I do not preach the gospel’ (1 Corinthians 9:16).
Palladius: So it seems; for you judge this very rightly.

Cyril: And besides these: ‘And you shall make,’ he says, ‘a plate of pure gold, and you shall engrave on it, as a seal is engraved, “Consecrated to the Lord.” And you shall set it on twisted blue thread, and it shall be on the turban; it shall be on the front of the turban. And it shall be on Aaron’s forehead, and Aaron shall take away the sins of the holy things, whatever the sons of Israel consecrate, of every gift of their holy things. And it shall be on Aaron’s forehead continually, acceptable for them before the Lord’ (Exodus 28:36–38). The turban, then, is of blue, and the plate is of gold. The engraving and the writing on it are the mystery of Christ and a clear proclamation, made beforehand, of his being sent into this world. For it says, ‘Consecrated to the Lord.’ Or did Emmanuel not say plainly that he had been consecrated by God the Father (John 10:36)?

Palladius: Yes; for I remember him saying to the Jews, ‘If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, “You are blaspheming,” because I said, “I am the Son of God”?’ (John 10:35–36)

Cyril: When the Son says that he has been consecrated by God the Father, he shows that he has been, as it were, appointed and sent. So ‘Consecrated to the Lord,’ he says; that is, a manifestation to this world and…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: §10 ends '…of the divine Gospel', §11 begins 'proclamation (κηρύγματος)'. 'Great high priest' (Hebrews 4:14) and 'having obtained eternal redemption' (Hebrews 9:12, which also has Christ entering the holy place once for all) are clear allusions; 'the spotless victim' may echo Hebrews 9:14 ('offered himself without blemish'), left uncited. Hebrews 10:14 quoted verbatim. πύργος, literally 'tower', here means the city's single ring of fortification; rendered 'wall'. συνοικίαι 'quarters' (blocks of dwellings); ἔλυτρον 'rind'; χιτῶνες ἰσχνοί 'thin membranes'. Ἁγίασμα Κυρίῳ (LXX 'Holy to the Lord', Hebrew 'Holiness to the LORD') rendered 'Consecrated to the Lord', and ἡγίασε / ἐνηγιᾶσθαι rendered 'consecrated', because Cyril's argument links the inscription to John 10:36 'whom the Father consecrated (ἡγίασεν) and sent'. In the last sentence Cyril writes the genitive Ἁγίασμα Κυρίου; same rendering. ὅσα ἂν ἁγιάσωσιν also 'consecrate' for consistency. Cyril's Exodus 28:36 reads 'ἐκτύπωμα σφραγίδος' ('as a seal is engraved'). μίτρα 'turban'. John 10:35–36 quoted closely (Cyril: 'Υἱὸς Θεοῦ' without article). 'Holy of Holies' = τὰ Ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων. Section ends mid-sentence: 'a showing forth into this world and…' + §12 '…a sending'.

title: Christ's kingship has no end; the linen headdress and belt
english: Cyril: …a sending, yet for kingship and glory. For in this way he brings Aaron to completion, setting the golden band on his forehead. And Christ is Lord and King of all, both by nature and by participation. For though he is God by nature, he emptied himself, lowering himself into the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7); and he receives kingship in the way that befits his human form, even though from above and from the beginning he sits beside God the Father, rules all things with him and is Master of all with him. Notice how his turban is made of blue and bears the bright token of kingship, I mean the golden plate. Blue is a sign of heaven; and remember that Christ says, ‘My kingdom is not of this world’ (John 18:36). For Christ is not an earthly king but a heavenly one, having the whole creation under his feet (Ephesians 1:22). And by adding, ‘And Aaron shall take away the sins of the holy things, whatever they consecrate, of every gift of their holy things’ (Exodus 28:38), he has clearly shown that all access and all perfecting are in Christ, and indeed that all justification is in him and through him, and also the putting away of former offenses. For he takes away our sins (John 1:29), and through him we have become acceptable, bringing offerings in spirit to God the Father (1 Peter 2:5).
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: And showing very well that our Savior’s kingship cannot be laid aside, but is continual and stretches into endless ages, he says of the plate on the turban, ‘And it shall be on Aaron’s forehead continually’ (Exodus 28:38). What then will become of the bold and senseless talk of the unholy heretics, who have babbled that Christ’s dominion will one day come to an end, and that Emmanuel will hand over the kingdom to God the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24) and leave the thrones of the Godhead? For they pride themselves on doctrines so dreadful and so short-lived; and it is fitting to say to them, ‘You are wrong, because you do not know the Scriptures’ (Matthew 22:29). For look, look: while God the Father plainly and clearly crowns Aaron with lasting glory and honor and with the tokens of kingship, they take the crown from him, and all but snatch away the sacred turban that graces his forehead.
Palladius: True.

Cyril: ‘And you shall make a headdress and a belt of fine linen’ (Exodus 28:39), he says. Aaron’s dress is that of a soldier, a belt and a helmet; for the headdress is shaped rather like a helmet. For Christ has fought for us ‘with a hidden hand’ (Exodus 17:16), as it is written; and ‘he has bent his bow and made it ready; he has fashioned his arrows for those who are burning’ (Psalm 7:12–13); and he has pulled down rulers, led powers in triumph (Colossians 2:15), shaken dominions, and rescued those on earth who were captives. And that the war he waged was not visible or material, nor, so to speak, against blood and flesh (Ephesians 6:12), seems to be shown in a riddle by this: that from linen alone, and that very…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: §11 ends 'ἀνάδειξις καὶ', §12 begins 'ἀποστολή'. ψαλίον (literally a band or curb-chain) is Cyril's word for the gold plate set on the forehead; rendered 'golden band'. τελειοῖ 'brings to completion' (the same verb the LXX uses for consecrating priests). 'Both by nature and by participation' (φυσικῶς τε ἅμα καὶ μεθεκτῶς) kept exact: Cyril explains it at once: as God he is King by nature; as man, having emptied himself, he receives kingship. κατά γε τὸ πρέπον τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ σχήματι echoes Philippians 2:7 (σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος), covered by the 2:7 citation. σύνεδρος, συγκατάρχων, συνδεσπότης rendered 'sits beside ... rules all things with him and is Master of all with him'. 'Having the whole creation under his feet' alludes to Psalm 8:6 (LXX 8:7) as applied to Christ in Ephesians 1:22 (also 1 Corinthians 15:27, Hebrews 2:8); cited as Ephesians 1:22. 'He takes away our sins' cited to John 1:29 (cf. 1 John 3:5). 'Acceptable ... spiritual offerings' cited to 1 Peter 2:5 (πνευματικὰς θυσίας εὐπροσδέκτους τῷ θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ). προσαγωγή rendered 'approach' (it can mean the bringing of an offering or access to God, cf. Ephesians 2:18, which is not cited). Exodus 28:38 quoted twice (Cyril's first quotation omits 'the sons of Israel'). The heretics who say Christ will hand back the kingdom and his rule will end are misreading 1 Corinthians 15:24–28; this was the teaching charged against Marcellus of Ancyra and Photinus, but Cyril names no one here, so no name is added to the text. Matthew 22:29 quoted in part. 'Crowns with lasting glory and honor' may echo Psalm 8:5 / Hebrews 2:9 ('crowned with glory and honor'); left uncited because Cyril's verb (ταινιόω) and setting differ. κίδαρις 'headdress', distinct from μίτρα 'turban' in §§11-12. Exodus 28:39 is a paraphrase ('κίδαρίν τε καὶ ζώνην ἐκ βύσσου ποιήσεις'; LXX 'κίδαριν βυσσίνην, καὶ ζώνην ποιήσεις'). 'With a hidden hand' is Exodus 17:16 in the LXX ('ἐν χειρὶ κρυφαίᾳ πολεμεῖ κύριος'), which differs from the Hebrew; cited there. Psalm 7:13–14 LXX = Psalm 7:12–13 in English Bibles; 'for those who are burning' follows LXX τοῖς καιομένοις. 'Led powers in triumph' cited to Colossians 2:15; 'pulled down rulers ... shaken dominions' and 'rescued ... captives' are not cited (no single verse; possible echoes of Ephesians 4:8 or Luke 4:18 are too loose). Ephesians 6:12 keeps Cyril's order 'blood and flesh'. Section ends mid-sentence ('ἐκ βύσσου μόνης τῆς ἄγαν' | §13 'ἰσχνῆς τὴν πολεμικὴν γενέσθαι σκευήν, κίδαρίν τε καὶ ζώνην'): whole sentence 'that his war gear, headdress and belt, was made from linen alone, and that very fine'.

title: The priests’ linen: holy warfare, purity, and putting off dead works
english: Cyril: …thin, that his war gear was made, the headdress and the belt. So with adornment fit for a priest he shows Aaron splendid and admirable. Then he gives a further command, saying: ‘And for the sons of Aaron you shall make tunics and belts, and you shall make headdresses for them, for honor and glory. And you shall put them on Aaron your brother, and on his sons with him. And you shall anoint them, and ordain them, and sanctify them, so that they may serve me as priests. And you shall make for them linen undergarments to cover the nakedness of their bodies; they shall reach from the loins to the thighs. And Aaron and his sons shall wear them whenever they go into the tent of witness, or whenever they come near to minister at the altar of the sanctuary. And they shall not bring sin upon themselves, so that they do not die. It is a perpetual statute for him and for his offspring after him’ (Exodus 28:40–43). You see that it befits Aaron’s descendants too to be seen, as it were, in the dress of war. For the whole sacred race is made for battle. It knows how to campaign and take the field, not against blood and flesh (Ephesians 6:12), but so as to hold back profane sin, fighting most openly and with reason for the doctrines of the truth, and ‘taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ’ (2 Corinthians 10:5), as it is written. They also have a linen undergarment, which covers very well what is unlovely and unseemly about the thighs. For all that belongs to the saints is truly dignified, and nothing unseemly is found in them. And the linen placed on the parts of the body around the thighs hints in some way that the cooling of the pleasures of the flesh is most fitting for the saints, for linen is cool. Heat that runs toward the most loathsome desires is foreign to everything holy. And there is another reason why those who have been allotted the priesthood wear robes and undergarments of linen. They must depart from dead works, and what is taken from a dead creature, I mean a sheep, is a symbol of deadness. So, again as in a type, to be clothed in garments of linen and not rather in garments of wool is the putting away of dead works; and this is the holy and perpetual law. And he made it plain that death must follow, wholly and without fail, for those who neglect what is fitting and the good order that most befits them, when, after saying what they must wear to perform the sacred service, he added: ‘And they shall not bring sin upon themselves, so that they do not die’ (Exodus 28:43).
Palladius: The law is sure. It shows very well what benefits each person, and it makes clear the means by which things would go best.

Cyril: So it is. With such a robe he adorns the sacred and chosen race, and he sanctifies it in another way as well: still as in shadow, yet in Christ. For it is written thus: ‘And these are the things you shall do for them to sanctify them, so that they may serve me as priests. You shall take one young bull from the herd and two unblemished rams, and unleavened loaves kneaded with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil. Of fine wheat flour…’ (Exodus 29:1–2)
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence from §12 (PG 68.748/749): the subject is Christ's war gear made 'of fine linen alone, very thin'. Exodus 28:40-43 is cited by English (Hebrew) verse numbers; in Rahlfs LXX the passage is numbered 28:36-39 because the LXX chapter is shorter. 'Ordain them' renders the LXX idiom ἐμπλήσεις αὐτῶν τὰς χεῖρας, literally 'fill their hands'. 'What is taken from a dead creature, I mean a sheep' renders σύμβολον δὲ νεκρότητος ὡς ἐκ θνησειδίου ληφθέν, φημὶ δὴ προβάτου; Cyril means wool, which he names in the next sentence. 'Dead works' echoes Hebrews 6:1 and 9:14, but Cyril uses the phrase as his own; no citation given. Linen-not-wool for priests recalls Ezekiel 44:17-18, which Cyril does not quote; no citation. 'Holy and chosen race' may echo 1 Peter 2:9 (γένος ἐκλεκτόν), but Cyril's words (ἱερὸν καὶ ἀπόλεκτον γένος) describe the Aaronic line here; no citation. The sentence beginning Ἕψεται δὲ ὅτι is loosely built in PG; rendered by its plain sense (death follows for those who neglect what is fitting, as the closing words of 28:43 show). The Exodus 29 quotation runs on into §14. κίδαρις/κιδάρεις and ζώνη/ζῶναι are rendered 'headdress(es)' and 'belt(s)' throughout, matching §12, because Cyril's point that Aaron's sons too wear 'warlike dress' rests on their having the same headdress (helmet) and belt as Aaron. PG Ἕψεται at the start of the last sentence of Cyril's turn is read as Ἕπεται ('it follows').

title: Washed, robed and anointed: baptism, Christ and the Spirit
english: Cyril: ‘…you shall make them, and you shall put them in one basket, and bring them in the basket, together with the young bull and the two rams. And you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the doors of the tent of witness, and wash them with water. And taking the vestments, you shall clothe Aaron your brother with the full-length tunic, the ephod and the breastpiece, and you shall join the breastpiece to the ephod for him. And you shall set the turban on his head, and set the holy plate on the turban. And you shall take some of the anointing oil and pour it on his head, and anoint him. And you shall bring his sons and clothe them with tunics, and gird them with belts, and put the headdresses on them. And they shall hold the priesthood for me for ever. And you shall consecrate the hands of Aaron and the hands of his sons’ (Exodus 29:2–9). So he ordered a young bull and two rams to be brought for sacrifice, with wafers and loaves in a basket. But he also purifies them beforehand in another way, setting the matter down, I think, as a type of true sanctification. For after washing Aaron with water, he clothes him in the holy robe. And when we too are washed through holy baptism and cleansed of every kind of uncleanness, it is then, then indeed, that we are enriched with the grace from above and from heaven, receiving the tunic of gladness, according to the words: ‘Put on our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 13:14). For our discourse has already shown that Christ was portrayed in many ways, as it were, in Aaron’s adornment. And he anoints his head with holy oil. David too sings somewhere: ‘You anointed my head with oil’ (Psalm 23:5), the oil signifying the gladness in hope of this voice of the saints, or else the visitation from above that makes us glad. For we who have believed have received mercy, and we are blessed by the Lord, our mind richly fed by the supply of the Spirit; and the head is a type of the mind. In this same way the priests were sanctified: washed with water and anointed with oil, and so anointed, putting on the sacred vesture and having their hands consecrated, so that they might now in some measure seem fit to offer the sacrifices purely and blamelessly from then on. We ourselves, too, sanctified beforehand, made glorious by the grace from above, and anointed for spiritual perfection, now bring our offerings to God with boldness, as it were with clean and wholly pure hands; spiritual offerings, clearly. And indeed I think something of this kind is shown by what blessed David sings about everyone who goes up to the mountain of the Lord: ‘innocent in hands and pure in heart’ (Psalm 24:3–4).
Palladius: So it seems.

Cyril: He then laid down by law how the sacrifices for the priests must be carried out, saying: ‘And you shall bring the young bull to the doors of the tent of witness, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the young bull before the Lord, at the doors of the tent of witness. And you shall slaughter the young bull before the Lord, at the…’ (Exodus 29:10–11)
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation of Exodus 29:2 from §13. LXX λογεῖον ('oracle') is rendered by the usual English 'breastpiece'; πέταλον τὸ ἁγίασμα as 'the holy plate'. τελειώσεις τὰς χεῖρας (literally 'you shall perfect the hands') is rendered 'consecrate the hands'; Cyril then speaks of the priests' hands being 'consecrated' (τελειούμενοι) and of believers 'anointed for spiritual perfection' (τελειότητα), so the Greek links consecration and perfection by one root. Romans 13:14: Cyril adds 'our' (ἡμῶν) to Paul's 'Put on the Lord Jesus Christ'. Psalm 23:5 is LXX Psalm 22:5; Psalm 24:3-4 is LXX Psalm 23:3-4 (the quoted words are from verse 4; 'goes up to the mountain of the Lord' paraphrases verse 3). 'The voice of the saints' is taken to mean the psalmist's voice as spokesman for the saints; the phrase is compressed in Greek. Possible but uncited echoes: 'tunic of gladness' (compare Isaiah 61:3, 10; Psalm 30:11), 'we have received mercy' (1 Peter 2:10), 'blessed by the Lord' (Psalm 115:15), 'supply of the Spirit' (Philippians 1:19), 'spiritual offerings' (1 Peter 2:5). The text in PG reads εὐλογγημένοι, a misprint for εὐλογημένοι. The Exodus 29:11 quotation runs on into §15.

title: The bull for sin, the ram of burnt offering, and the ram of consecration
english: Cyril: ‘…doors of the tent of witness. And you shall take some of the young bull’s blood and put it on the two horns of the altar with your finger, and you shall pour out all the rest of the blood at the base of the altar. And you shall take all the fat on the belly, and the lobe on the liver, and the two kidneys and the fat on them, and put them on the altar. But the flesh of the young bull, and its hide, and its dung you shall burn with fire outside the camp, for it is a sin offering. And you shall take one of the rams, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the ram’s head. And you shall slaughter it, and taking the blood you shall pour it out against the altar all around. And you shall cut the ram into pieces limb by limb, and wash the entrails and the feet with water, and put them on the pieces with the head. And you shall offer up the whole ram on the altar, a whole burnt offering to the Lord, for a fragrant aroma; it is an incense offering to the Lord. And you shall take the second ram, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the ram’s head. And you shall slaughter it, and take some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron’s right ear, and on the tip of his right hand, and on the tip of his right foot, and on the lobes of the right ears of his sons, and on the tips of their right hands, and on the tips of their right feet. And you shall take some of the blood from the altar and some of the anointing oil, and sprinkle it on Aaron and on his robe, and on his sons and on his sons’ robes with him; and he and his robe shall be sanctified, and his sons and his sons’ robes. And you shall pour out the ram’s blood against the altar all around. And you shall take from the ram its fat, and the fat that covers the belly, and the lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys and the fat beneath them, and the right shoulder, for this is a consecration; and one loaf made with oil, and one wafer from the basket of unleavened bread set out before the Lord. And you shall put them all on the hands of Aaron and on the hands of his sons, and you shall set them apart as a special portion before the Lord. And you shall take them from their hands and offer them up on the altar of burnt offering for a fragrant aroma before the Lord; it is an offering to the Lord. And you shall take the breast from the ram of consecration, which is Aaron’s, and set it apart as a special portion before the Lord, and it shall be your share. And you shall sanctify the breast as a special portion, and the shoulder of the contribution, which has been set apart and which has been taken from the ram of consecration, from Aaron and from his sons. And it shall be for Aaron and his sons a perpetual statute from the sons of Israel; for this is a special portion, and it shall be a contribution from the sons of Israel, from the sacrifices of deliverance of the sons of Israel, a contribution to the Lord’ (Exodus 29:11–28). And a little further on: ‘And you shall take the ram of consecration and boil its flesh in a holy place, and Aaron…’ (Exodus 29:31–32)
translator_notes: The whole section is Cyril's quotation of Exodus 29 (LXX), opening mid-verse at 29:11 and breaking off mid-verse at 29:32; it continues in §16 through 29:34. 'And a little further on' marks Cyril's skip of 29:29-30. Cyril's text reads 'the two horns of the altar' (ἐπὶ τῶν δύο κεράτων) where the LXX of 29:12 has 'the horns'; kept as he quotes it. As in the LXX, the pouring of the second ram's blood around the altar comes after the sprinkling (Hebrew 29:20-21 has the reverse order). 'For it is a sin offering' renders ἁμαρτίας γάρ ἐστι (literally 'for it is of sin'). LXX terms: βραχίων 'shoulder' (Hebrew 'thigh'); τελείωσις 'consecration' (literally 'completion, perfection'); ἀφόρισμα 'special portion' (Hebrew 'wave offering'); ἀφαίρεμα 'contribution' (Hebrew 'heave offering'); κάρπωμα 'offering'; θύματα τὰ σωτήρια 'sacrifices of deliverance' (Hebrew 'peace offerings'). In 29:26 'it shall be your share' is addressed to Moses. No commentary by Cyril falls in this section. the quotation breaks after 'Aaron' (Greek ἔδονται Ἀαρὼν καὶ οἱ); §16 resumes 'and his sons shall eat', which supplies the verb ἔδονται.

title: The ordination meal; Christ the calf burned outside the camp
english: Cyril: …‘and his sons shall eat the flesh of the ram and the loaves in the basket at the doors of the tent of witness. They shall eat the things by which they were sanctified, to consecrate their hands and to sanctify them; and no stranger shall eat of them, for they are holy. And if any of the flesh of the sacrifice of consecration or of the loaves is left until morning, you shall burn what remains with fire. It shall not be eaten, for it is a holy thing.’ (Exodus 29:32–34)
Palladius: How deep a thing the commandments of the law are!

Cyril: Very deep indeed; you were right to say so. Yet they are not wholly obscure, since the Holy Spirit makes the divine light flash within us. Come, then, let us again speak of each point as best we can. Our Lord Jesus Christ sanctifies us in countless ways, and makes us sacred and acceptable. For through him and in him we have gained access (Romans 5:2), and we are not unwelcome to God the Father. For us who are subject to corruption and sin, his death is most needful and necessary for salvation; so too is his life, and besides these the perfecting that comes through his body and blood; for perfection is in Christ, not in the law (Hebrews 7:19).
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: See, then, how the things by which we have been so fully saved and sanctified, and have become sacred and holy in Christ, are still set out in types. A young calf from the herd was brought for sacrifice, and it is slaughtered at the very doors of the holy tent after hands have been laid on it. Its blood was poured out at the altar, and the horns of the altar were smeared with it; the inward parts are sent up in smoke, ranked with the most fragrant offerings of incense; and the rest of the body is carried out beyond the camp and burned (Exodus 29:10–14). Christ is the calf, as one both free of the yoke and under the yoke. For though he is God by nature, he came under the law because of his humanity (Galatians 4:4). Is not a young calf unused to the yoke, and yet of a nature made to bear the yoke?
Palladius: It is so.

Cyril: Christ, then, is again called a calf in keeping with the plan of salvation, so that we may grasp at one and the same time both that the Godhead of the Word is a stranger to servitude, and that in his humanity he came to be in a nature that bears the yoke. He is slaughtered, as it were, for the holy tent and for those who laid their hands on him; and these are Levites and priests. For he died for the Church and for those consecrated to him through faith. That the death of Emmanuel is sacred, and acceptable to God the Father as a sacrifice, you may see from the blood poured out at the holy altar and smeared on it, and from the inward parts burned as incense. These may stand as a type of the virtues that lie within and belong to the mind. In these virtues there is a spiritual fragrance, and not in one way only, since the inward parts are many: the fat, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver (Exodus 29:13). What is left of the body is burned outside the camp. For Christ suffered outside the gate; so Paul writes (Hebrews 13:12). And the consuming of the body by fire would signify, in a subtle way, that his suffering and death…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation; the quotation began in section 15 at Exodus 29:31 ('and Aaron and…'), so the part here is Exodus 29:32–34 LXX. τελείωσις / τελειῶσαι: inside the Exodus quotation, which runs on from section 15, the term is rendered 'consecration / consecrate' to match section 15's 'ram of consecration'; in Cyril's own comment it is 'perfecting / perfection', because he plays on it ('perfection is in Christ, not in the law'). 'we have gained access' (τὴν προσαγωγὴν ἐσχήκαμεν) matches Romans 5:2 word for word; Ephesians 2:18 is a close parallel, not cited separately. 'perfection is in Christ, not in the law' cited to Hebrews 7:19 ('the law made nothing perfect') as a clear allusion. The calf rite Cyril summarises is Exodus 29:10–14 (hands laid on, slaughter at the door, blood on the horns, fat/kidneys/liver lobe burned, flesh burned outside the camp). οἰκονομικῶς rendered 'in keeping with the plan of salvation' (the economy of the Incarnation). ἰσχνῶς rendered 'in a subtle way' (the fine-drawn spiritual reading named at the start of Book 11). Section breaks mid-sentence; it continues in section 17.

title: Death turned to glory; the first ram and Christ's holy life
english: Cyril: …would in no way end in dishonor, but would issue in bright and most evident glory. For the divine nature is thought of under the form of fire, and in this way it came down upon Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18). To destroy the power of death (Hebrews 2:14), Christ underwent death in keeping with the plan of salvation, so that he might be glorified by us as God. His death, then, passes on into a glory fit for God, having as its end a glorious return to life; and the lowliness of his suffering, overcome by the highest honors, vanishes into nothing. And this, I think, is what is meant in a veiled way by the dead calf being consumed by fire. And when he adds, ‘for it is a sin offering’ (Exodus 29:14), he has made known that the suffering of Christ took place for the cleansing away of sin; and the matter is not obscure.
Palladius: Indeed it is not.

Cyril: Next the first ram is taken and slaughtered in the same way as the calf. Its blood again was poured out at the altar, and it was cut up limb by limb and offered up together with its head and feet, after its inward parts had been washed with water, because it is an offering of incense (Exodus 29:15–18). By these things again Christ is portrayed for us: he who is perfect, pictured in the perfect ram, and whose life is holy. The pouring of the blood at the altar shows this, I think, for blood is a type of life; and it shows him dedicated to God the Father as a fragrant aroma, on behalf of all together and of each one. The ram’s being offered up on the altar both whole and limb by limb is again a type of this. Now we are members of Christ individually, and all of us are understood to be one body (1 Corinthians 12:27; Romans 12:5). That he is holy and sacred through and through, and has no spot of uncleanness, the washing of the inward parts makes very plain. The head and the feet are offered up together, showing that the Savior’s life was fragrant in holiness from the beginning to the very end. For in every animal the head is the beginning, while the feet are the end, where the whole body, as it were, comes to its close. Or perhaps it is better to take the head as a type of the mind, and the feet as a type of the course of active, practical life. In Christ all is fragrant, and both his thoughts and his deeds reached the height of purity; for he committed no sin (1 Peter 2:22). That is why it calls the dedication of the ram whole burnt offerings and a sacrifice (Exodus 29:18): he is not holy or sacred only in part. For it would in no way befit him, but rather us, to be weak at times and to be caught stumbling; for no one is pure from sins, and we all stumble in many ways, as it is written (James 3:2).
Palladius: And how might one suppose that the very life of Christ was also for our sake?

Cyril: You will see it quite easily if you consider that we became sharers in the transgression that took place in Adam, and all but paid the penalty for his offences ourselves, since the curse ran through to all (Romans 5:12), and the wrath was in some way spread over the race descended from him. So the Only-begotten came down to become man and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and…
translator_notes: 'for it is a sin offering': LXX Exodus 29:14 ἁμαρτίας γάρ ἐστιν, quoted by Cyril as ἁμαρτία γάρ ἐστιν ('for it is sin'); rendered 'sin offering' because Cyril's point is the cleansing of sin. The subject of ἐπειπών is unstated (the lawgiver/text); kept as 'he'. 'destroy the power of death' (καταλύσων τοῦ θανάτου τὸ κράτος) cited to Hebrews 2:14 as a clear allusion. First ram rite = Exodus 29:15–18 (limb by limb, inward parts and feet washed, head included); θυμίαμα in LXX 29:18 rendered 'offering of incense'. 'blood is a type of life' echoes Leviticus 17:11 (Deuteronomy 12:23), but Cyril makes it a typological rule rather than a quotation: uncited. 'no spot of uncleanness' (σπίλον) may echo Ephesians 5:27 or 1 Peter 1:19: uncited, doubtful. 'no one is pure from sins' may echo Job 14:4 LXX or Proverbs 20:9: uncited; 'we all stumble in many ways' is James 3:2 verbatim (πολλὰ πταίομεν ἅπαντες). 'the divine is conceived under the form of fire' may echo Deuteronomy 4:24 / Hebrews 12:29: uncited. 'the Only-begotten … dwelt among us' (ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν) = John 1:14. Section breaks mid-sentence; continues in section 18. Romans 5:12 is placed beside 'the curse ran through to all' (διαδραμούσης εἰς ἅπαντας, echoing εἰς πάντας ... διῆλθεν), not beside the wrath clause.

title: The obedient Son; the second ram and the ear that tests words
english: Cyril: …placed himself in subjection to God the Father. ‘For he became obedient to the point of death’ (Philippians 2:8), blotting out the charges of the rebellion that came from Adam; and he brought the fragrance of his ready obedience to God the Father on behalf of all together and of each one, and through him we have been saved. Paul is a witness, writing thus: ‘So then, as through one trespass there came condemnation to all people, so also through one righteous act there comes justification that brings life to all people. For as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous’ (Romans 5:18–19). Do you see, then, that we have been saved as in the calf, since Christ died for us, while we give off a fragrance to God the Father through his submission and his life in holiness? For the blood of the ram was poured out at the holy altar.
Palladius: I understand what you are saying.

Cyril: In many ways it portrays the same one for us, as in shadows. ‘And you shall take,’ it says, ‘the second ram’ (Exodus 29:19), and its slaughter is carried out as with the first. Aaron is anointed, and the band of priests under him is sanctified, as the blood is put on the tips of the right hand and ear, and of the right foot as well (Exodus 29:20). The vestment of the priests too is sanctified by being sprinkled with the blood (Exodus 29:21). Then, after the rest has been poured out at the base of the altar, as God saw fit, the inward parts are taken, with an unleavened loaf and one wafer, both made with oil (Exodus 29:22–23). Aaron and those with him place these in their own hands and bring them, and Moses receives the sacrifice and offers it up (Exodus 29:24–25). Besides this, he said that the shoulder and the breast must be assigned to the priest and counted among the portions set apart (Exodus 29:26–28). The name of the victim is ‘ram of perfection’ (Exodus 29:26). When the inward parts have been burned as incense, the rest of the body is eaten with the loaves, and whatever has been left until morning is burned with fire (Exodus 29:31–34). For so the sacred text runs.
Palladius: How deep the passage is!

Cyril: You are right; it is very deep indeed, but it is in labor with the mystery of Christ. For he became for us a ram of perfection, making us fully fitted for every good thing, and most outstanding in virtues through sanctification in the Spirit. And before all else he planted in us a hearing full of blessing, that is, one that is obedient and easily guided, well fitted to receive the doctrines about him, but that will not bear the whispered chatter and foul, unbridled talk of those who fight against the truth and set themselves against the doctrines of right belief. For this is the fruit of holy hearing. And indeed the divine John speaks to us somewhere in this way: ‘Brothers, test the spirits, whether they are from God; every spirit that does not confess Jesus Christ is not from God, and every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ is from God’ (1 John 4:1–3). And the testing of words would rightly be done by nothing so much as by the ear. Holy…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence (the subject is the Only-begotten from section 17). Philippians 2:8 is quoted with γέγονε for γενόμενος. Romans 5:18–19 quoted nearly verbatim; the elliptical Greek ('to all men unto condemnation') is filled with 'there came / there comes', as in standard English versions. Second ram rite = Exodus 29:19–28: blood on right ear, hand and foot (29:20; Cyril lists hand, ear, foot in that order and the order is kept), sprinkling of Aaron and the vestments (29:21), fat with one loaf and one wafer from the basket (29:22–23), placed in the hands of Aaron and his sons and offered by Moses (29:24–25), breast and shoulder set aside (29:26–28); the eating and the burning of leftovers is 29:31–34, already quoted in sections 15–16. The name 'ram of perfection' (κριὸς τελειώσεως) is LXX 29:26–27, 31 (29:22 LXX has only 'for this is a perfection'), cited to 29:26; kept as 'perfection' here, against 'consecration' in the Exodus quotation of sections 15–16, because Cyril's next speech plays on it ('making us fully fitted', ἀρτίως ἔχοντας). οἱ ἀμφὶ τὸν Ἀαρών rendered 'Aaron and those with him' (i.e. Aaron and his sons). ἀφαιρουμένων = the portions removed (the LXX 'ἀφαίρεμα', heave offering) rendered 'portions set apart'. 1 John 4:1–3 is quoted loosely: Cyril has 'Brothers' (ἀδελφοί) where the New Testament reads 'Beloved', and he gives the negative clause (4:3) before the positive (4:2); his order and wording are kept. 'Sanctification in the Spirit' may echo 2 Thessalonians 2:13 / 1 Peter 1:2: uncited, common phrase. 'πολυτρόπως' may echo Hebrews 1:1: uncited. 'the testing of words … by the ear' probably echoes Job 12:11 / Job 34:3 LXX ('the ear tests words'), but Cyril does not mark it as Scripture: uncited, possible allusion. ὀρθότης rendered 'right belief'. Section breaks mid-sentence ('Holy…'); section 19 continues 'then, will the ear be…'.

title: Ear, hand and foot made holy; the holy food kept from outsiders
english: Cyril: …then, will the ear be for those who care for precision and right doctrine. Yet this is the gift of Christ, a gift of welcome from heaven, and what the holy blood has accomplished; for in him and through him we possess every excellent thing. For this reason the hand also was sanctified, which points to active work, and the foot as well, a clear symbol of walking straight in one’s paths (Exodus 29:20). For we ought to take pride in holy works and walk well along the path that leads to everything pleasing to God, as is sung in the Psalms, ‘And I turned my feet to your testimonies’ (Psalm 119:59), or as the book of Proverbs says, ‘Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways’ (Proverbs 4:26). Let the sacred and chosen race, then, possess a holy hearing, and likewise a holy hand and foot, in the ways we have just described.
