All are anointed on the right side, and as it were at their farthest part, that is, at the tips; for he speaks of the tip of the ear, and of the foot and the hand as well. For every good action, I think, is noble and belongs to the right; it has nothing of the left, as wickedness has, and it reaches to the tips, that is, all the way through, even to the end. For those consecrated to God ought to stand on the right in holiness, persevering to the very end. ‘For he who began a good work in you,’ it says, ‘may he bring it to completion’ (Philippians 1:6). It is quite out of place, too, to fall back in some way, shrinking from carrying the good through to its end. Since Moses stands as a type of God, Aaron and those with him bring the sacrifice, and Moses himself receives it (Exodus 29:24–25). By this too God was, as it were, signifying that he will receive, almost straight from their hands into his own, the sacrifices offered in Christ by those so sanctified, and will not scorn the gift; for it carries the fragrance of Christ. And this, I think, is the meaning of the inward parts offered up and burned as incense to him. The portion set apart for the priest from the ram of consecration is the breast and the arm (Exodus 29:26–28). The arm would be a symbol of strength, and the breast of the heart and the kidneys. And Christ has been given to the holy and priestly race by God the Father as power and wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). Or are we not wise in him, and very strong?
Palladius: Of course we are. For it is written that Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), has become these things for us from God (1 Corinthians 1:30).

Cyril: The meat is holy food for those chosen for the sacred service. It is given together with the unleavened loaves, and no one of another race shares in it (Exodus 29:32–33); or, if anyone should do so, he would die. For it befits holy souls to share in holy food, that is, in the body of Christ, and the blessing is closed to those of another race. By ‘of another race’ one may understand the race that is still unbelieving and unbaptized, and besides these, whoever has been twisted into heterodox thinking, is at odds with the convictions of the saints, and has been cut off, as it were, by the wickedness of its doctrines. And whatever is left of the sacrifice is consumed by fire…
translator_notes: PG 68.761. Section opens mid-sentence: the first word of the sentence, Ἅγιον ('Holy'), stands at the end of §18; The English begins '…then, will the ear be' so the join reads 'Holy … then, will the ear be'. Section ends mid-word (λεί|ψανον); 'whatever is left' is rendered here and the clause continues in §20. LXX Psalm 118:59 = English Psalm 119:59. Proverbs 4:26 follows the LXX wording ('make straight paths… direct your ways'). Philippians 1:6: Cyril's text reads the imperative ἐπιτελεσάτω ('may he bring it to completion') where the New Testament has the future ἐπιτελέσει; rendered as printed. Exodus 29:20: blood on the tip of the right ear, right thumb and right big toe (parallel Leviticus 8:23–24, not cited because Cyril is reading Exodus 29). βραχίων: LXX word for the portion English Bibles call 'thigh' or 'shoulder' (Exodus 29:27); kept 'arm' because Cyril reads it as a symbol of strength. In Exodus 29:26–28 the breast is Moses' portion and the 'arm' of the removal goes to Aaron and his sons; Cyril calls both the priest's portion. δεξιός/σκαιός pun (right/favourable, left/ill-omened) rendered 'belongs to the right… nothing of the left, as wickedness has'. 'He would die': Exodus 29:33 forbids the outsider to eat but names no death penalty; no citation given for that clause (compare Leviticus 22:9–10; Numbers 18:7, doubtful). 'The fragrance of Christ' may echo 2 Corinthians 2:15; uncited as doubtful. 'The body of Christ' as holy food: no specific verse cited (1 Corinthians 10:16 is not a clear allusion).

title: Nothing kept till morning; the anointing and the seven days
english: Cyril: …since the law does not allow it to be eaten on into the next day (Exodus 29:34). For there will be for us, I think, another way of sanctification in the age to come, worked spiritually and no longer bodily, in a manner known to God, who reshapes all things and changes them into whatever he wills. A mind not without understanding will follow the argument: once the corruption in us has been undone, after we have come back to life from the dead, the things through which one could escape it are perhaps in some way no longer needed. Another way of sanctification, fitting the condition of that time, will then be devised, when Christ is with us. Having said what came to mind, we will yield to those who understand better. And perhaps the divine Paul hints at something of this kind when he says, ‘But when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away’ (1 Corinthians 13:10), meaning that it will have an end and cease.
Palladius: So it seems.

Cyril: These, then, are the things he said must be carried out for the consecration of the priests. With the priests of Israel gathered together and assembled into a congregation, he laid down how they were to be publicly installed, saying, ‘Take Aaron and his sons, and the oil of anointing, and the calf for sin, and the two rams, and the basket of unleavened bread, and assemble the whole congregation at the door of the tent of witness. [And Moses did as the Lord had commanded him, and assembled the congregation at the door of the tent of witness.] And Moses said to the congregation, “This is the word which the Lord commanded to be done”’ (Leviticus 8:2–5). Then he clothes Aaron in his adornment, and the priests as well (Leviticus 8:7–9, 13), and with the oil of anointing he sprinkles the altar seven times, and all its vessels, and the laver, it says, and the tent and all that is in it, ‘and he sanctified them’ (Leviticus 8:10–11). For the tent is holy, and the altar is fully enriched with the sanctification that comes through the Spirit, though it does not share in it as one ranked among rational beings does; for it is not holy in the way that, say, the nature of an angel or a human soul is holy, but as it were through contact with the sacrifice laid upon it. For holy too is any place where Christ may be. Having anointed the altar seven times, that is, abundantly, he sanctifies Aaron; for he poured the oil of anointing over him (Leviticus 8:12). Besides this, he brought the sacrifices for Aaron and for his sons in the ways we have just set out (Leviticus 8:14–29). When these things had been completed, he gave a further command, saying, ‘And you shall not go out from the door of the tent of witness for seven days, until the day is fulfilled, the day of your consecration. For seven days he will consecrate your hands, as he did on this day, as the Lord commanded to be done, so as to make atonement for you; and at the door of the tent of witness you shall sit seven days. Day and night keep the charges of the Lord, so that you do not die; for so the Lord God commanded me’ (Leviticus 8:33–35).
translator_notes: PG 68.764. Section opens mid-word (λεί|ψανον, 'remainder', at the end of §19); The English begins '…since the law does not allow it to be eaten on the next day as well', continuing §19's 'whatever is left of the sacrifice is consumed by fire'. τυχόν ('perhaps') stands beside 'after coming back to life from the dead'; read as Cyril's tentative tone about the whole inference (he goes on to 'yield to those who understand better') and placed with 'are perhaps… no longer needed', so the English does not seem to doubt the resurrection. τῶν ἱερῶν τελείωσιν taken as 'the consecration of the priests' (masculine 'sacred persons'); a neuter reading 'completion of the rites' is possible. 'The priests of Israel gathered… into a congregation' kept as printed; the quotation itself assembles the whole congregation. Leviticus 8:2–5: PG prints Leviticus 8:4 in square brackets as an editorial supplement after 'And Moses said to the congregation', and the bracket ends by repeating 'And Moses said'. The English keeps the supplement in brackets, places it in its Leviticus order, and drops the repeated 'And Moses said'. Cyril's quotation omits 'and his garments' from Leviticus 8:2; not supplied. 'Then he clothes Aaron… and he sanctified them' is Cyril's paraphrase inside the quotation (present/future verbs, 'it says'); Leviticus 8:10–11 has Moses anoint the tent, sprinkle the altar seven times and anoint its vessels and the laver. 'He brought the sacrifices': Leviticus 8:14–29 (bull of the sin offering, ram of burnt offering, ram of consecration). Leviticus 8:33–35 follows the LXX: 'consecrate your hands' is the LXX for the Hebrew idiom 'fill your hands' (ordain); Cyril's punctuation joins 'day and night' to keeping the charges.

title: Staying within the tent; the eighth day begins
english: Cyril: The account has shown us well enough what was done in the case of each of the sacrifices. So let us stop going into these matters in fine detail and turn to this point. The law does not allow those who have been enriched with a holy and chosen lot, and have now been consecrated for the priesthood, to go anywhere outside the holy tent (Leviticus 8:33). It bids them sit within until the seventh day (Leviticus 8:35), and all but nails them to the doors, so that they do not cross the threshold. In this, I think, it makes their sitting in holy places a symbol of steadfastness and of remaining in holiness. For we who have been appointed to wait upon God must be firmly set and unshaken in virtue, not straying outside the fitting way nor running away from the mind that befits a priest, but always near God and, as it were, dwelling with him, as was said through the voice of a prophet: ‘Seek earnestly, and dwell with me’ (Isaiah 21:12). Moses ordered this to be done for seven days; the seven signifies that we must be eager to wait upon God at every season, for in a way it means ‘throughout’ and ‘always’. While they are inside the tent, he commands them to keep the charges of the Lord (Leviticus 8:35), hinting that obedience is the fruit of waiting upon God, together with the will to do whatever he may choose to command. This is how we must wait upon the Master of all, since carelessness about what is good always ends in the very last of evils. That is why, as I believe, Moses added, ‘so that you do not die’ (Leviticus 8:35).
Palladius: You have spoken rightly.

Cyril: Aaron, now consecrated for the sacred service, begins to carry out what was prescribed. And in what way, come, let us say. For it is written again in Leviticus: ‘On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel; and Moses said to Aaron, “Take for yourself a young calf from the herd for sin, and a ram for a whole burnt offering, without blemish, and offer them before the Lord. And speak to the elders of Israel, saying: Take one male goat for sin, and a young calf and a lamb a year old for a whole burnt offering, without blemish, and a calf and a ram for a sacrifice of salvation before the Lord, and fine flour mixed with oil; for today the Lord will appear among you.” And they took them, as Moses commanded, before the tent of witness, and the whole congregation came forward, and they stood before the Lord. And Moses said, “This is the word which the Lord has spoken; do it, and the glory of the Lord will appear among you.” And Moses said to Aaron, “Approach the altar, and make your sin offering and your whole burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself and for your house; and offer the gifts of the people, and make atonement for them, as the Lord commanded”’ (Leviticus 9:1–7). If you bring a keen mind to the sacred Scriptures, Palladius, you will see the mystery of Christ shining clearly here too.
Palladius: In what way?
Cyril: On the eighth day (Leviticus 9:1) Moses, as it were, ceases from acting as priest, and Aaron begins…
translator_notes: PG 68.765. The section opens a new sentence inside Cyril's turn from §20, so it carries the 'Cyril:' label. Isaiah 21:12: Cyril quotes the LXX ('if you seek, seek, and dwell with me'; his text reads ζητῶν ζήτει, 'seek earnestly'); English Bibles from the Hebrew read differently ('If you will inquire, inquire; come back again'), so the citation follows the LXX wording. 'Until the seventh day' renders εἰς ἑβδόμην ἡμέραν, Cyril's paraphrase of the seven days of Leviticus 8:33–35. PG misprints ἱερουργίαν as ἱερουγρίαν; read as 'sacred service'. Leviticus 9:1–7 follows the LXX: γερουσία rendered 'the elders'; θυσία σωτηρίου (the peace offering of English Bibles) rendered 'sacrifice of salvation' because Cyril later reads it of Christ; ὁλοκάρπωσις and ὁλοκαύτωμα both rendered 'whole burnt offering'; χίμαρον ἐξ αἰγῶν ἕνα rendered 'one male goat'. 'Make your sin offering' renders ποίησον τὸ περὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας σου. The last sentence breaks off ('Aaron begins…'); §22 continues 'yet Moses has not fallen silent'.

title: Christ's priesthood begins on the eighth day
english: Cyril: …yet Moses has not fallen silent, even though Aaron is already hurrying to the works of the priesthood. For the time of Christ's priesthood may rightly be understood as the time after the law, that is, the eighth day, on which the resurrection took place, and which is, as it were, the beginning of a new age. For in Christ there is a new creation, as it is written (2 Corinthians 5:17). Once Christ has been revealed on the eighth day, the things of Moses come to an end, for we no longer worship in types and shadows (Hebrews 8:5). Yet the teaching of the law has not fallen silent, for the law is spiritual to those who are spiritual (Romans 7:14), and it always speaks of the mystery of Christ. Moses, then, promised that on the eighth day the glory of the Lord would be seen (Leviticus 9:1–6), for the law announced beforehand the time of our Savior's coming. Again he gives a further command: Aaron is first to offer sacrifices for himself, and after this those for the whole people (Leviticus 9:7). In this, I think, he already makes the matter in some way a type for those of our own day, and indicates very well and clearly that it is right and fitting for those chosen for the priesthood, and for those who receive sanctification in faith, to be holy and consecrated. What the manner of the offering was, we shall explain as best we can. A young calf, then, was slaughtered for sin and for the cleansing of those who performed the sacred rites. Its blood was poured out at the holy altar, the inner parts were turned to smoke, and the rest of the body was burned up with fire (Leviticus 9:8–11). A ram, in turn, was what was burned whole, according to the customary law of the whole burnt offering (Leviticus 9:12–14). A male goat was the victim for cleansing the people's sin (Leviticus 9:15); a young calf and a lamb were for the whole burnt offering (Leviticus 9:3, 16); a ram and a calf were for the sacrifice of salvation (Leviticus 9:4, 18), and fine flour was also laid on the altar, though perhaps not all of it, only a handful, a part of it (Leviticus 9:17). Then it says: ‘And Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them; and he came down after making the sin offering, the whole burnt offerings and the sacrifices of salvation. And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of witness, and they came out and blessed all the people; and the glory of the Lord appeared to all the people. And fire came out from the Lord and consumed what was on the altar, both the whole burnt offerings and the fat portions; and all the people saw it, and were amazed, and fell on their faces’ (Leviticus 9:22–24).
Palladius: What, then, do you say about this as well?

Cyril: In truth the glory of the Lord was seen on the eighth day; that is, the Son, the glory of God the Father, became manifest. For God named him so when he said to the most holy Moses, ‘As I live, says the Lord, all the earth shall surely be filled with the glory of the Lord’ (Numbers 14:21). It is he himself who makes us consecrated. He is slain for us, like the calf; he sets us free from sin, releases us from every charge, and scours away the filth that comes from being condemned. He likewise, like the ram, is made perfect for a pleasing spiritual aroma; he himself becomes the sacrifice of salvation and sanctifies us with his own blood (Hebrews 13:12); he himself is the fine flour moistened with oil, in the gladness of a holy life, presenting himself for us to God the Father (Ephesians 5:2).
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence, continuing the end of section 21 ('and Aaron begins…'); the speaker label is kept for the reader. The Greek ἥ γε μὴν ἐννόμῳ παίδευσις is read as ἔννομος παίδευσις, 'the teaching of the law'. Romans 7:14: Cyril adds 'to the spiritual' to Paul's 'the law is spiritual'. Hebrews 8:5 cited for 'worship in types and shadows' (Paul: ὑποδείγματι καὶ σκιᾷ λατρεύουσι); Hebrews 10:1 is a further possible echo, uncited. Leviticus 9:1–6 covers the eighth day (9:1) and the promise that the Lord's glory would appear (9:4, 9:6). θυσία σωτηρίου is the LXX term for the Hebrew peace offering; rendered 'sacrifice of salvation' to match the sibling sections and Cyril's later reading of it as Christ. μοσχάριον = 'young calf', μόσχος = 'calf', kept distinct as in Leviticus 9:2–4 LXX. Numbers 14:21: Cyril's wording (ἢ μὴν ἐμπλησθήσεται … πᾶσα ἡ γῆ) differs from the common LXX text (ἐμπλήσει ἡ δόξα κυρίου πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν) and lacks 'and my name lives'; the sense is the same. τελειούμενος 'made perfect' may play on the ram of consecration (κριὸς τῆς τελειώσεως, Leviticus 8:22); uncited. Ephesians 5:2 cited for the closing clause: ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν … τῷ Θεῷ … εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας matches Paul's 'gave himself for us … to God for a fragrant aroma'; παραδεικνύς may be a corruption of παραδιδούς. Hebrews 13:12 cited for 'sanctifies … with his own blood' (ἵνα ἁγιάσῃ διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος).

title: Priests and people offer themselves to God
english: Palladius: I understand what you mean.

Cyril: For my part, I think that the sacrifice for Aaron and for the people neatly hints at the consecration of the saints to God. Emmanuel has now been revealed and has made plain all that concerns him; through him we have been called to sanctification, made acceptable and consecrated, and dedicated to the Father for a fragrant aroma. For notice that, through the rites just described, the perfecting of the priests was carried out according to the law, while it was through him, in turn, that they were sanctified in many ways. For he was burned like a calf outside the camp for sin (Leviticus 9:11); he was offered up in smoke like a ram duly burned whole, all of him, limb by limb, as though for each one and for all (Leviticus 9:13); and he sanctified them by anointing them with blood, as the ram of salvation. Now that the eighth day has dawned, that is, the day on which the glory of Christ became more manifest, when death was abolished and corruption trampled down, priests and people alike bear fruit for God. They do not honor him with things foreign to them, nor delight the Master of all with things from outside, as Israel according to the flesh did (1 Corinthians 10:18), but they show themselves to be a fragrant sacrifice. For in a way, as if in the likeness of the victims, we offer up our own souls in sacrifice and bring them to God. We die to the world and to minding the things of the flesh (Romans 8:5), we endure the putting to death of the passions, and we are all but crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:19–20), so that, passing over to a holy and blameless life, we may live as he wills. The inspired Paul, too, writes something of this kind: ‘Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our body’ (2 Corinthians 4:10). And again: ‘If we endure, we shall also reign with him’ (2 Timothy 2:12). If we are conformed to his death and his sufferings, as it is written, we shall share in the resurrection and the glory as well (Philippians 3:10–11). So then Christ suffered for us outside the gate, as the blessed Paul says, and we too go out of the gate, bearing his reproach (Hebrews 13:12–13); slain in the same way, like a young calf, and burned whole like a ram, we make our life in Christ fragrant to God. These, then, are the victims offered for Aaron and for those with him and descended from him. For the people, a male goat is the sin offering (Leviticus 9:15). And why is that, when a young calf was offered for the cleansing of the priests? Everything that belongs to the priests stands higher: the bringing of sacrifices and the rites of cleansing and purification. And a young calf is larger in body than a goat, and so displays a clear token of the spiritual pre-eminence found in the realities themselves. The young calf and the lamb for the whole burnt offering (Leviticus 9:3) hint at the infancy in Christ of those consecrated in faith. The calf and the ram signify very well endurance and courage, and fruitfulness in gentleness: the calf is the type of the first, the ram of the second (Leviticus 9:4). The fine flour soaked with oil (Leviticus 9:4) shows very clearly the bright hope of the life in Christ. For it is not in gloom and tears…
translator_notes: Section ends mid-sentence; the clause is completed at the start of section 24. 'Through him' (δι' αὐτοῦ) in 'sanctified through him in many ways' is read as Christ, since the following clauses describe Christ as calf, ram and ram of salvation. 'He sanctified them by anointing them with blood, as the ram of salvation' is left uncited: the blood-anointing of the priests belongs to the ram of consecration (Leviticus 8:22–24; also Leviticus 8:30 and Exodus 29:20–21), not the ram of the peace offering in Leviticus 9:4, 18; Cyril's label is kept as written. 'Limb by limb' (μελειστί) matches the burnt offering cut in pieces in Leviticus 9:13. 'Called to sanctification' may echo 1 Thessalonians 4:7; 'dedicated to the Father for a fragrant aroma' may echo 2 Corinthians 2:15; 'death abolished' may echo 2 Timothy 1:10; 'bear fruit for God' may echo Romans 7:4; 'a fragrant sacrifice' of ourselves may echo Romans 12:1; 'dying to the world' may echo Galatians 6:14; 'putting to death of the passions' may echo Colossians 3:5. All these are possible allusions only and are uncited. 1 Corinthians 10:18 cited because 'Israel according to the flesh' is Paul's phrase in a passage about sacrifices. Galatians 2:19–20: Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι is 2:19 in the Greek text and 2:20 in the KJV, hence the range. Philippians 3:10–11 cited for 'conformed to his death … sufferings … resurrection'; Romans 8:17 ('glorified with him') is a possible second source for 'glory', uncited. Hebrews 13:12–13 is quoted loosely (Hebrews has 'let us go out to him outside the camp'); Cyril attributes Hebrews to Paul, as was usual in his time. ὁλοκάρπωσις (Leviticus 9:3 LXX) and ὁλοκαύτωσις are both rendered 'whole burnt offering'. Leviticus 9:3 has the young calf and lamb; Leviticus 9:4 has the calf, the ram and the fine flour mixed with oil. In the typology 'the first' is endurance and courage (calf), 'the second' fruitfulness in gentleness (ram).

title: Fire from the Lord, and Aaron's blessing
english: Cyril: …but in good cheer and gladness that we ought to hold fast to the life in Christ. For this, I think, is the meaning of ‘Come, let us rejoice in the Lord’ (Psalm 95:1). For so the glory of Christ will shine out purely and clearly, welcoming most gladly the fruits the saints bring, just as then, too, God came down visibly in the form of fire and consumed the sacrifices (Leviticus 9:24). He all but counts the approved life of those sanctified in faith as his food and delight. The passage also hints at a mystery. For then God sent the blaze of fire down upon the divided pieces, as though in some way touching what lay before him, for the Godhead always takes on the guise of fire. But now, when the spiritual sacrifice is set before him, he touches what lies before him in a spiritual way, not in the form of fire but in the Holy Spirit, and makes it life-giving for those who desire to partake of it; and we have received this by faith as true.
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: Aaron lifted up his hands and blessed the people (Leviticus 9:22). And see again: here, through Aaron, is as it were the first laying on of hands upon the people. For the true Aaron blesses everyone, priests and people, the small together with the great, as it is written (Psalm 115:13), all but laying his hands on them as well; and the laying on of the hand would be a clear sign of the all-holy Spirit coming down upon us. Before Aaron's priestly service there was no laying on of hands. ‘For the Spirit was not yet,’ as John says, ‘because Jesus was not yet glorified’ (John 7:39).
Palladius: That is convincing.

Cyril: He also sets in order the form of the priests' prayer in this way, making its words very aptly foretell something of what would come to us through Christ. For he said: ‘Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying: Thus you shall bless the sons of Israel, saying to them. And they shall put my name upon the sons of Israel, and I the Lord will bless them. May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine upon you, and give you peace, and have mercy on you’ (Numbers 6:23–27). So he commands those crowned with the priesthood to bless the people, but he usefully keeps them from rash thinking by showing that it is not a human hand that blesses, but he himself, as Lord. For ‘every good gift and every good present and every blessing is from above, coming down from the Father of lights,’ as it is written (James 1:17). And Christ is the way of the blessing; he is the one who distributes the heavenly goods to us, and in him and through him all things come from the Father. Indeed the inspired Paul says, ‘Grace to you and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 1:7). So we are blessed in the name of God; and, aptly indicating how this too might come about, he said that the priest who prays over the people must pronounce: ‘May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make…’ (Numbers 6:24–25)
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence, completing the last clause of section 23; the speaker label is kept for the reader. ἐξῆφθαι (ἐξάπτω) is taken as 'be attached to, cling to' the life in Christ, not 'be kindled'. 'Come, let us rejoice in the Lord' is LXX Psalm 94:1, English Psalm 95:1. 'The small together with the great' is LXX Psalm 113:21, English Psalm 115:13. διχοτομήματα, 'divided pieces', is a sacrificial term (Exodus 29:17 LXX; Genesis 15:17 LXX, where fire passes between the pieces); Cyril applies it to the Leviticus 9:24 offering; uncited. 'The Godhead always takes on the guise of fire' may echo Deuteronomy 4:24 / Hebrews 12:29 ('God is a consuming fire'); uncited. The 'spiritual sacrifice' now touched by the Holy Spirit and made life-giving reads as a reference to the Eucharist; the translation keeps Cyril's words without naming it. νοητός is rendered 'spiritual' (perceived by the mind, as opposed to the visible sacrifice). John 7:39: 'For the Spirit was not yet' keeps the Greek without adding 'given'. Laying-on of hands as sign of the Spirit's coming may allude to Acts 8:17–18; uncited. τῶν διὰ Χριστοῦ παθημάτων is rendered 'what would come to us through Christ': πάθημα here means what is undergone or experienced, though 'sufferings' is a possible reading (section 25 explains the blessing as loosing the curse). Numbers 6:23–27: Cyril's quotation is compressed and reordered: he places 'they shall put my name … I will bless them' (6:27) before the blessing, and gives the blessing as 'bless and keep; face shine; give peace; have mercy', omitting 'lift up His face' here (he quotes the full form at the end of this section and in section 25). James 1:17: Cyril reads 'every good present' (δώρημα ἀγαθόν, for τέλειον) and adds 'and every blessing'. Romans 1:7 cited for Paul's greeting, which recurs in 1 Corinthians 1:3, 2 Corinthians 1:2 and elsewhere; Cyril's 'our Lord' is a small variant. 'Christ is the way of the blessing' may echo John 14:6, and 'in Him and through Him all things' may echo Colossians 1:16 or 1 Corinthians 8:6; both uncited. The section ends mid-quotation; the blessing (Numbers 6:24–26) is completed in section 25.

title: The priestly blessing fulfilled in Christ: mercy and peace
english: Cyril: ‘…his face shine upon you, and have mercy on you; the Lord lift up his face upon you, and give you peace’ (Numbers 6:25–26). The blessing, then, keeps us, for it undoes the curse and refashions what had sinned, so that in Christ it may be found worthy of praise. Paul is witness to this, for he wrote: ‘Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love he predestined us for adoption through Christ to himself’ (Ephesians 1:3–5).

You see that rejection came about through sin, and that man is accepted for adoption when he is blessed in Christ by sharing in the Spirit, whom he also poured out on us richly (Titus 3:6); he does not give the Spirit to the saints in part, but places him in them as from his own fullness. And the shining of God’s face would at once bring us mercy, if indeed it is true that our share in eternal life comes in through knowing God. For so the Savior said to his Father and God in heaven: ‘And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent’ (John 17:3).

That the Son, who has also shone upon us, is the face of God the Father, no one, I think, could doubt in the least. For he is his exact imprint (Hebrews 1:3), his likeness and his image (Colossians 1:15), and through him and with him we know the Father; and with such knowledge our receiving mercy necessarily comes in as well. For we have been justified by faith, and not by works of righteousness that we ourselves did, but according to his great mercy (Titus 3:5). We have laid down the burden of corruption and have been changed into newness of life in Christ (Romans 6:4), because God has taken pity on us.

In another way too, if we turn the force of the passage toward the Jews, they truly received mercy when the Only-begotten shone upon them. For the law lay on them like a burden hard to bear and fit only to be cast off, the law that condemns and punishes sinners without pity (Hebrews 10:28). But they received mercy, gaining through Christ, late and with difficulty, the grace that justifies. Longing to see his coming, they had cried out to the God of all: ‘O God of hosts, bring us back, and make your face shine, and we shall be saved’ (Psalm 80:7). So we have all received mercy in the shining forth of Christ.

And further, the lifting up of God’s face brings peace. Christ is the giver of that peace and the one who awards it, for he sets it before those who believe in him and bestows it on them as his own good. ‘My peace,’ he says, ‘I give to you; my peace I leave with you’ (John 14:27). For when the Father set the Son, as it were, on high, granting him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9) and saying, ‘Sit at my right hand’ (Psalm 110:1), then, yes then, we put an end to the enmity that divided us and were joined together in peace, by choosing to set our minds on what is his and to walk in the Spirit…
translator_notes: The section opens mid-word (ἐπι|φάναι) inside the Aaronic blessing begun at the end of §24 (Numbers 6:24–26 LXX); speaker remains Cyril. 'The blessing keeps us safe' renders Φυλάττει, which picks up φυλάξαι σε of Numbers 6:24. 'Ὁρᾷς ὅτι τὸ ἀπόβλητον διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἔφυ' is syntactically difficult (perhaps ἔφυγε, 'rejection has fled', was intended); rendered as 'rejection came about through sin', which keeps the printed ἔφυ. The Spirit is neuter in Greek (ὃ … αὐτό); rendered 'whom … him'. Titus 3:6 (ἐξέχεεν … πλουσίως) and Titus 3:5 are close verbal allusions. 'Image' could also echo 2 Corinthians 4:4; Colossians 1:15 cited. 'Without pity' (οἰκτιρμοῦ δίχα) cited to Hebrews 10:28 (χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν) as a clear verbal echo; 'burden hard to bear' may echo Acts 15:10 but is not cited. LXX Psalm 79:8 = English Psalm 80:7 (the refrain also at 80:3, 80:19; 'God of hosts' form matches 80:7). LXX Psalm 109:1 = English Psalm 110:1. John 14:27 is quoted with its two clauses in reverse order; translated as Cyril has it. Ephesians 1:5 is quoted with 'through Christ' (διὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ) for the NT's 'through Jesus Christ'. 'The enmity that divided us' may echo Ephesians 2:14–16, but there Christ is the one who ends the enmity, while Cyril's participle has 'we' as subject; left uncited, agency kept as printed. 'Walk in the Spirit' (Galatians 5:16, 25; Romans 8:4) is a general Pauline phrase, left uncited here; Galatians 5:16 is quoted and cited in §27. βραβευτής rendered 'awarder' (one who gives the prize); a possible echo of Colossians 3:15 (βραβευέτω) is left uncited. The sentence runs on across the column break: περιπα|τεῖν; 'to walk in the Spirit' is completed here and §26 resumes with the relative clause.

title: Peace through the exalted Son; the cleansing of the Levites
english: Cyril: …in whom and through whom we have been shown to be sharers in the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), since Christ binds us together into unity. For he said somewhere to the Father: ‘I desire that, just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us’ (John 17:21–22). For, as Scripture says, ‘we are all one body in Christ’ (Romans 12:5), and ‘whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit’ (1 Corinthians 6:17). And that we have been enriched with peace toward him when God the Father, as it were, lifted up his own face, that is, glorified the Son, he himself will make plain when he says: ‘When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself’ (John 12:32).
Palladius: You think rightly. ‘For he is our peace’ (Ephesians 2:14), ‘and through him we have gained access in the Spirit to the Father’ (Ephesians 2:18).

Cyril: This, then, is what the law tells us about the priests and how they were appointed. It also says that the Levites must be thoroughly sanctified, and only then, once purified beforehand in the proper ways, take up the ministry assigned to them. In Numbers it says this: ‘Take the Levites from among the children of Israel, and purify them. And this is how you shall perform their purification: you shall sprinkle them with water of purification, and a razor shall pass over their whole body, and they shall wash their garments, and they shall be clean. And they shall take one young bull from the herd, and with it its sacrifice of fine flour mixed with oil; and you shall take one young bull a year old from the herd for a sin offering. And you shall bring the Levites inside the tabernacle of testimony. And you shall gather the whole congregation of the children of Israel, and you shall bring the Levites forward, and Aaron shall set the Levites apart as an offering before the Lord from the children of Israel, so that they may do the works of the Lord. And the Levites shall lay their hands on the heads of the bulls, and you shall offer the one as a sin offering and the other as a whole burnt offering, to make atonement for them. And you shall set the Levites before the Lord, and before Aaron, and before his sons, and you shall give them over as an offering before the Lord. And you shall separate the Levites from among the children of Israel, and they shall be mine. And after this the Levites shall go in to do the works of the tabernacle of testimony’ (Numbers 8:6–15).
Palladius: Explain clearly, then, how we should understand the manner of purification applied to the Levites.

Cyril: It is a mystical one, Palladius, and once again it is in Christ. For he is our cleansing, the washing away of every stain, and the giver of sanctification. ‘For you shall sprinkle them,’ it says, ‘with water of purification’ (Numbers 8:7). This is just what the wise Paul made plain when he wrote: ‘For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who have been defiled, sanctify for the purity of the flesh, how much more the blood of Christ’ (Hebrews 9:13–14). And the saying is true. For if there is benefit in the types, and the shadow brings salvation, how could the truth, that is, the blood of Christ, not do so far more? So the water of purification, mixed with the ashes of the heifer (Numbers 19:9, 17), was a clear symbol of what is called the dying of Christ…
translator_notes: The section opens mid-word (περιπα|τεῖν); 'in whom and through whom' refers to the Spirit (ᾧ/οὗ). John 17:21–22 is quoted loosely, with 'I desire' (θέλω) as at John 17:24. 'One body in Christ' matches Romans 12:5; 1 Corinthians 10:17 is close but lacks 'in Christ'. 'Peace toward him' (τὴν πρὸς αὐτὸν εἰρήνην): the pronoun most likely means God the Father but could mean the Son; left as 'him'. Palladius' second quotation blends Ephesians 2:18 with Romans 5:2 (ἐσχήκαμεν τὴν προσαγωγήν); cited to Ephesians 2:18. τὸ Λευιτικόν here means the Levitical order or tribe, not the book of Leviticus (the passage quoted is Numbers); rendered 'the Levites'. The Numbers quotation is LXX Numbers 8:6–15 with these differences from the standard LXX: 'inside' (ἔνδοσθεν) the tabernacle for ἔναντι ('before'); Numbers 8:10b (the Israelites laying hands on the Levites) and 'before the Lord' in 8:10a are absent; 'to the Lord' is absent from 8:12. Translated as Cyril's text stands. ἀπόδομα rendered 'offering' (something given over to God). Cyril calls Hebrews the work of Paul; kept as he says it. 'Water of purification mixed with the ashes of the heifer' joins Numbers 8:7 to the heifer rite of Numbers 19:9, 17 (where the water is 'water of sprinkling'); cited as a clear allusion. The final sentence crosses the column break (σύμ|βολον ἐναργὲς ἦν, opening §27); for readable English the whole clause 'was a clear symbol of what is called the dying of Christ' is completed here, and §27 resumes with the relative clause. νέκρωσις rendered 'dying', as in 2 Corinthians 4:10.

title: Ashes, razor and washing: dying with Christ
english: Cyril: …that dying which we ourselves also pray to fulfill in holy baptism, through faith. For, as the inspired Paul himself said somewhere, once again: ‘For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life’ (Romans 6:4). And he said again: ‘Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be made manifest in our mortal flesh’ (2 Corinthians 4:10–11).
Palladius: And what, then, is the dying of Christ spoken of here?

Cyril: To have died to the world and to sins, and to live out a life that is sacred and holy and as dear to God as possible. Paul again took great pride in this, when he said: ‘For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me’ (Galatians 2:19–20). This, I think, is what it means to have died to the world and to have undergone the dying of Christ, and in turn to live out the life that is in him. So the heifer’s ashes mixed with water (Numbers 19:17) would point to the dying of Jesus as it is accomplished in holy baptism. And he said that even those who served in the Levitical order must share in it, once they had cast off, again as in a shadow, every kind of uncleanness of the flesh.

For this, I think, is shown very clearly by the shaving of the body’s hair with a razor (Numbers 8:7). For ‘the word of God is living and active and sharper…’ (Hebrews 4:12), and it cuts away from the mind, as one would hair and nails, the uncleanness of the impulses of the flesh that are inborn in us. Holy Scripture somewhere calls this a law of sin dwelling in the members of the flesh, waging war against the law of the mind, and dragging us toward what is forbidden (Romans 7:23). But cut as with a razor by the power and working of the Holy Spirit, it grows weak, and even if it somehow springs up again in us, it is all the more quickly shorn away. For, ‘walk by the Spirit,’ he says, ‘and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh’ (Galatians 5:16).

Just as the razor does not tear our hair out from the very root once and for all, but cuts it straight away as it grows back, so too the word of God in us does not tear out, root and all, the movement of desire that is as though inborn in us (for perfect holiness is reserved for the age to come). Rather, it puts that movement to death as it grows back and springs up in us, and it tames the law that runs wild in the members of the flesh. So the removal of the hair hints at the cleansing of the mind, which the divine and sharper word of God works in us. And the washing of the garments points to a bright and genuine way of life for us, the one that is seen outwardly. For, as it is written, ‘taking thought for what is good, not only before the Lord but also before people’ (2 Corinthians 8:21). And the Lord himself says somewhere: ‘Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good…’ (Matthew 5:16).
translator_notes: The section opens mid-word (σύμ|βολον ἐναργὲς ἦν); that main clause is rendered at the end of §26, and this section resumes with the relative clause ('that dying which…') so the English reads cleanly; the repeated 'that dying' is the only connective added, and it restates the Greek antecedent. 'In holy baptism' and 'through faith': Cyril says we pray to fulfill the dying of Christ through faith, in baptism. Romans 6:4 is quoted without 'from the dead'. 2 Corinthians 4:10–11 is quoted as one sentence, taking 'mortal flesh' from verse 11. The second ἐκτεθνάναι has ἐν κόσμῳ ('in the world') where the first has the plain dative κόσμῳ; both rendered 'died to the world' as the sense requires. 'He said' (ἔφη) of the Levites refers to the lawgiver speaking in Numbers 8. 'Bodily uncleanness' renders ἀκαθαρσία σαρκική ('fleshly'); 'bodily impulses' renders σαρκικὰ κινήματα. The relative ὃν ('which … Scripture calls a law of sin') points forward to νόμον; the subject of 'grows weak' and 'is shorn away' is that law of sin. Romans 7:23 cited; the 'dwelling' language also recalls Romans 7:17, 20. Galatians 5:16 is quoted with the imperative 'walk' (περιπατεῖτε), as in the NT. 2 Corinthians 8:21 matches Cyril's wording ('before the Lord … before men'); Romans 12:17 and Proverbs 3:4 LXX are related but lack this exact form. 'The Lord himself' renders αὐτός, whose antecedent is Κυρίου just quoted; the words are Christ's (Matthew 5:16). The quotation breaks off at 'your good…' and continues with 'works' in §28.

title: The two calves and the people's hands on the Levites
english: Cyril: …works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven’ (Matthew 5:16). So it must be that those who are truly holy and consecrated carry about in their own body, purely both within and without, the dying of Jesus (2 Corinthians 4:10), and are in some way joined with him through holy baptism.
Palladius: You have spoken well.

Cyril: He said that the sacrifice for them must be offered with two calves, one full-grown and one a year old, that is, tender and young (Numbers 8:8). The full-grown one is for the whole burnt offering, and fine flour mixed with oil is burned together with it; the other, for sin, is burned outside the camp (Leviticus 4:12), for that is how the sacrifices for sin are completed. And here again Christ is in both. In the calf for the whole burnt offering he is wholly holy and a sweet-smelling fragrance to God the Father on our behalf (Ephesians 5:2), bringing to the saints the delight and gladness of the life that is in hope; for the fine flour mixed with oil was offered up together with the calf, and it will surely, I think, follow those who have honored the life that is in Christ. He is also the young calf for sin, consumed by fire, for ‘by his wound we were healed’ (Isaiah 53:5), as the Scriptures say. Notice that the full-grown calf is burned whole, while the yearling is slaughtered for sin (Numbers 8:12), so that through the two you may understand at once the One: most fragrant in a spiritual sense, as in the perfection of virtues, and slaughtered, as in simplicity and innocence. For he says: ‘I, like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, did not know’ (Jeremiah 11:19). The laying on of hands by the people of Israel would show that the priestly race is brought to God as an offering on behalf of all and from all together. For he says: ‘The sons of Israel shall lay their hands on the heads of the Levites’ (Numbers 8:10). The Levites laid their hands on the heads of the sacrificial victims, which were slaughtered on their behalf as a type of Christ (Numbers 8:12). They did this not to bless them in any way, far from it, but as though by the laying on of hands to point to the God who bears our sins (Isaiah 53:4) and is offered in sacrifice for us, so that he might nail to his own cross the record of debt that stood against us (Colossians 2:14). You will understand that the people’s ordination of the Levites was carried out in the same way. For when they laid their hands on them, it was as though they were setting them before God in their own place for the sacred service, as chosen men. Then, the laying on of hands was the practice. But now that things have passed over to what is incomparably better, the people vote for those who are called through Christ to the sacred service, joining heartily in the cry that they are worthy; and they do this in the churches, just as, of course, those of old performed the laying on of hands upon the Levites at the sacred and divine tabernacle (Numbers 8:9). It is plain, then, that if an ordination took place neither in church nor in the presence of the people, it would be contrary to the divine will and outside the sacred laws. Once the Levites have been consecrated, they handle everything that belongs to the sacred service (Numbers 8:15).
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation of Matthew 5:16 begun at the end of §27. συντεθειμένους (as printed: 'joined/put together with') may be a corruption of συντεθαμμένους 'buried with', which would echo Romans 6:4 quoted in §27; translated as printed ('joined with him') and Romans 6:4 left uncited here. The two calves follow Numbers 8:8 LXX (the first calf with its grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; the second ἐνιαύσιος περὶ ἁμαρτίας); Numbers 8:12 assigns one to sin and one to the whole burnt offering. Numbers 8 does not say the sin-offering calf is burned outside the camp; Cyril applies the general rule for sin offerings (Leviticus 4:12; also 4:21), hence the Leviticus citation. Hebrews 13:11-12 is a natural background but Cyril does not draw it; uncited. 'A sweet-smelling fragrance on our behalf to God' cited to Ephesians 5:2 (ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ... τῷ θεῷ εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας), a close verbal match. ἕψεται taken as future of ἕπομαι 'will follow'; its subject is understood as the delight and gladness just named. Isaiah 53:5 LXX τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἡμεῖς ἰάθημεν (cf. 1 Peter 2:24); 'wound' renders μώλωψ (bruise, stripe). Jeremiah 11:19 is quoted from the LXX with γάρ for δέ. Numbers 8:10 LXX reads 'on the Levites'; Cyril's 'on the heads of the Levites' blends in the wording of 8:12, kept. 'The God who bears our sins' cited to Isaiah 53:4 LXX (οὗτος τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει; English Bibles from the Hebrew read 'griefs'). Colossians 2:14 is adapted (Cyril: 'to His own cross'). κεῖρας in the print is a misprint for χεῖρας. χειροτονία rendered 'ordination', χειρῶν ἐπίθεσις and χειροθεσία 'laying on of hands'. ἀσυγκρίτως taken with εἰς τὸ ἄμεινον ('incomparably better') despite the Migne comma; it could also qualify ἐπιψηφίζονται. παραφωνοῦντες ... ὡς εἶεν ἄξιοι refers to the people's acclamation 'worthy' at ordination. 'Before God in their own stead' alludes to the Levites taken instead of the firstborn (Numbers 8:16-18) but too loosely to cite. 'At the sacred and divine tabernacle' cited to Numbers 8:9 (the Levites brought before the tent and the congregation gathered). 'Take up all the duties of the sacred service' cited to Numbers 8:15 (after this the Levites shall go in to do the work of the tent; cf. 8:22). τετελειωμένοι rendered 'consecrated'. Numbers 8:12 cited a second time for the Levites laying their hands on the calves' heads (the verse names both acts). χειρόγραφον rendered 'record of debt' rather than the older 'handwriting'. ἅπτονται rendered 'handle' so the contrast with §29 'will not touch the divine altars' stays visible.

title: Whoever is not holy must keep away from the altar
english: Cyril: So then, whoever is not holy in Christ and does not first purify himself in the way that is fitting, let him keep far away; for he will not touch the divine altars without punishment.
translator_notes: Continues Cyril's turn from §28; the Greek gives no new speaker. καθ' ὃν ἂν πρέπει τρόπον has ἄν with an indicative (as printed); rendered 'in the way that is fitting'. 'Keep far away' and the warning about touching holy things may echo Numbers 18:3-4 or Leviticus 22:3, but there is no clear verbal match; uncited. Book 11 ends with this sentence at PG 68.781: the heading of Book 12 follows directly in the print.
